typicalHomeowner.text: A DUBLIN FAMILY BRINGING A PARENT HOME. They have a rear garden of a reasonable size, an existing house they can link services to, and a relative who needs a bedroom, a bathroom and a front door of their own. The 2026 provision is what makes the project feasible for them, and they are working within its window rather than treating it as permanent. THEY WILL BE COMPARING TIMELINES AS MUCH AS PRICES. NOT FOR: a household whose only available space is to the side or front of the house, where the route does not apply; nor for a couple needing two bedrooms.

A HOUSEHOLD ACCOMMODATING TWO PEOPLE RATHER THAN ONE — both parents, or an adult child and partner — with a large rear garden and a long-term intention. They want the unit to work for years, not as a stopgap, which is why the extra 12 m2 over the 1 Bed matters to them. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST EXPOSED TO THE CEILING RISK, and should be the most insistent on written confirmation of the as-built area and measurement basis. NOT FOR: a small garden, where 45 m2 plus the retained private open space will not fit; nor for a buyer who wants certainty above space.

A FAMILY SOLVING A LONG-TERM HOUSING PROBLEM RATHER THAN A TEMPORARY ONE — an adult child with a partner and a child of their own, or two relatives who each need a bedroom. They have a large rear garden, a multi-year horizon, and have accepted that the project is a building rather than a purchase. THEY ARE WILLING TO GO THROUGH PLANNING, which is what distinguishes them from every other buyer in this range. NOT FOR: anyone whose priority is speed or certainty; the 45 m2 or 33 m2 models exist for them. NOT FOR a small garden, where 48 m2 plus retained open space will not fit.

A HOUSEHOLD BUILDING A WELLNESS CORNER IN THE GARDEN. Often the same buyer who is also looking at a cold plunge or hot tub, and who thinks of the sauna as equipment rather than as a building. They are choosing on heat, timber and appearance, and they will be guided by the supplier's own material because Atlas holds nothing technical for this model. THE ADVICE THAT MATTERS MOST TO THEM is structural rather than thermal: because the sauna counts toward the same 30 m2 allowance as any other garden building, they should decide now whether a garden office or studio might follow, and reserve the allowance accordingly. NOT FOR: anyone whose primary need is a work or study room.

A WELLNESS BUYER, NOT A WORKSPACE BUYER. Someone adding a sauna to a garden as a lifestyle purchase — often alongside a hot tub or plunge tub — who is choosing on heat performance, timber quality and appearance rather than on square metres per euro. They are typically not comparing this against a garden office at all, and they should not be shown one as an equivalent. THE THING THEY MOST NEED TO KNOW is the thing they are least likely to ask: the footprint counts against the same 30 m2 back-garden allowance as any other building, so a sauna now may cost them a garden room later. NOT FOR: anyone needing a work, study or habitable room — this is a single-function wellness building.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE, and inventing a profile from a company name would be exactly the kind of guess this layer exists to prevent. THE ONE THING THAT CAN BE SAID ABOUT THE BUYER: anyone pursuing this record will be starting the specification conversation from scratch rather than choosing from a documented range, so it suits a homeowner who is happy to ring a supplier, ask direct questions and work from a written quotation — and who is not trying to compare three products side by side on a spreadsheet, because this one cannot join that comparison yet.

SOMEONE WANTING A SCULPTURAL GARDEN BUILDING FOR DAYTIME USE — a studio, a reading room, a home office with character — rather than accommodation. That intention is what keeps the Class 3 route open to them, and it is worth stating explicitly when they enquire. A NORTHERN IRELAND BUYER HAS THE SIMPLER POSITION, with supplier and applicable rules in one jurisdiction; a Republic buyer takes on both a cross-border purchase and a different planning regime. NOT FOR: overnight use, which would put this product in the same position as the Lodge and the Hut; nor for a buyer needing confirmed dimensions before enquiring.

SOMEONE ADDING GUEST OR LETTING ACCOMMODATION, MOST OFTEN ON A RURAL OR NORTHERN SITE. A holiday let, a self-contained space for visiting family, or a small hospitality venture — the uses a lodge is designed around. A NORTHERN IRELAND BUYER IS THE MOST NATURAL FIT, since the supplier and the applicable rules are then in the same jurisdiction. A REPUBLIC BUYER TAKES ON TWO EXTRA QUESTIONS — cross-border supply and a different planning regime — and should resolve both before ordering. NOT FOR: a homeowner wanting an exempt garden office, which this product cannot be.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS CHARACTER RATHER THAN SQUARE METRES. A writing room, a quiet retreat at the end of the garden, or occasional guest space on a rural site — the hut is chosen for what it is, not for how much floor it provides. THE DECISIVE QUESTION FOR THEM IS WHETHER GUESTS WILL SLEEP IN IT, because that single answer moves the project from exempt to not. A Northern Ireland buyer has the simpler position on jurisdiction. NOT FOR: a working office needing desk space and storage; nor for a buyer who wants the planning position settled before speaking to the supplier.

SOMEONE WITH AN AWKWARD GARDEN AND A CLEAR HEAD ABOUT NUMBERS. A homeowner working around a boundary, a mature tree, a slope or an existing outbuilding, who has already measured what is there and knows how much of the 30 m2 allowance remains. They are comfortable commissioning rather than shopping, and they will judge the supplier by the quality of the quotation rather than by a brochure. THEY MUST BE PREPARED TO ASK FOR WHAT IS NOT PUBLISHED: external footprint, finished height, wall and roof build-up, glazing, warranty and what the price includes — none of it is held in Atlas. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to compare three products side by side this week, since this record cannot join that comparison.

A physiotherapist, massage therapist, counsellor, beautician or similar practitioner moving a practice out of rented rooms and into their own garden, within haulage range of Cork and with a garden a crane can reach. The finish standard is the reason they are here: clients judge a treatment room the moment they walk in, and a factory-built, engineer-certified unit removes the variability of an on-site build. They understand that comfort for a client lying still for an hour is a different requirement from comfort for someone working at a desk, so they will specify the heating themselves rather than assume it, and they will ask about acoustic separation because privacy is a professional obligation, not a preference. Above all they will take planning advice on change of use before ordering, because clients visiting the property is not incidental use. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone relying on the exemption without settling the use question; anyone without crane access; anyone who needs the footprint confirmed before committing.

Someone commissioning a small independent unit on their own land — accommodation for a family member, a self-contained studio, a let — rather than a garden office, and who has taken planning advice BEFORE approaching the supplier rather than after. They are within haulage range of Cork, have crane access, and are budgeting at residential rather than garden-building levels: press coverage puts a 25 m2 bathroom-and-kitchenette unit at EUR 60,000-70,000. They value that the building arrives factory-finished and engineer-certified, with concealed plumbing done under controlled conditions rather than in a garden. They will establish the external footprint, the planning route, who makes the water and drainage connections, and which warranty covers the sanitaryware as against the structure. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone relying on the garden-structure exemption, which this configuration is unlikely to meet at any size; anyone without crane access; anyone wanting a plain office and paying for a bathroom and kitchen they will not use.

An Irish homeowner — realistically within haulage range of Bandon, Co. Cork — who wants one building to do two jobs: a properly built year-round office and secure integral storage, without a separate shed taking a second bite out of the same planning allowance. They are buying construction quality rather than a headline price: SIPS with PIR insulation, engineer sign-off before dispatch, a twenty-year guarantee from a manufacturer with twenty years behind it. They have a garden a crane can reach and stand in, and they are prepared for a six-to-eight-week custom build rather than an off-the-shelf delivery. Before ordering they will get three things in writing: the TOTAL external footprint including the store, whether the base is inside the price, and whether the twenty years covers this configuration. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone without crane access, which rules the product out entirely; anyone who needs to test the planning exemption before committing; anyone comparing on price per square metre, which cannot be calculated.

An Irish homeowner within haulage range of Cork who does not yet know exactly what the building will be used for over its life — an office while the children are small, a studio or hobby room later — and wants a shell good enough to outlast every one of those uses. They are buying the construction, not a floor plan: SIPS with PIR insulation, engineer certification before dispatch, a twenty-year guarantee. They have a garden a crane can reach and stand in, and they accept a custom six-to-eight-week build. They understand that flexibility carries a planning obligation — the exemption depends on the use staying incidental and the building never being slept in — and they will be specific with the planning authority rather than relying on 'multi use' as cover. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone without crane access; anyone who needs the area confirmed before committing, since none is published; anyone whose intended use is residential, which this route does not support.

NOBODY SHOULD BE SHORTLISTING FROM THIS RECORD IN ITS CURRENT STATE. A buyer interested in Lasita Maja should work from the nine models that carry a verified internal floor area, and — if a workspace is the brief — from the New York, the only one the manufacturer lists for workshop and office use. THE RECORD'S VALUE IS AS A FLAG that a catalogue entry can outlive the product it describes. NOT FOR: any buyer, until the model is confirmed as still on sale and a specification is obtained.

SOMEONE COMFORTABLE BUYING A SHELL AND FINISHING IT PROPERLY. Nineteen square metres under a gable roof is a good room, and a buyer who understands that the headline price buys timber — not a roof covering, not insulation — can build something genuinely year-round for a total they can calculate in advance, because Gardenhouse24 publishes the option prices. THEY WILL VISIT LIMERICK OR WEXFORD before deciding. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing the EUR 6,171 headline against an insulated turnkey room; nor for anyone who assumes a roof covering is included.

Someone in the north-east or Dublin corridor with a requirement that has already failed a catalogue search — a garden that is the wrong shape, a plot with no crane access, a use that combines two things, a height requirement no standard model meets, or simply a strong view about how the building should look. They are comfortable being the client on a design, not the customer on a purchase: they will arrive with dimensions, a use description and a list of what must be specified, rather than expecting the supplier to have decided it. They value the showroom, the short build and the staged payments, and they accept that the quality of the outcome depends on the quality of their own brief. Before the 10 per cent deposit they will have the drawing, the insulation build-up, the electrical schedule, the base position and the warranty term in writing. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who wants a specification handed to them; anyone comparing on published evidence, since none exists for this product.

A family in Co. Down, Co. Louth, Co. Meath or the Dublin commuter belt whose house has run out of room and who has priced a rear extension and flinched at both the cost and the months of disruption. They want a warm, finished room for sitting, entertaining or giving teenagers somewhere of their own, and they are content that it is a separate building rather than an extra room off the kitchen. They value being able to walk into a showroom and see the finish before committing, and they are comfortable specifying size and layout themselves rather than picking from a catalogue. They will do three things before paying the 10 per cent deposit: get a dimensioned drawing, get the warranty document, and ask whether the base is in the price. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who needs to compare published specifications before making contact, since none exist; anyone wanting overnight accommodation, which the no-habitation condition excludes; anyone outside the north-east or Dublin corridor without confirming coverage first.

Someone in the north-east or Dublin corridor who trains at home several times a week and is replacing a gym membership rather than supplementing one. They own or intend to own a rack, a bench and probably a treadmill, so they know that clear height and floor behaviour decide whether the building works — and they are choosing a bespoke builder precisely because those are the two things they can specify here and cannot elsewhere. Their garden likely rules out a craned pod. They are prepared to arrive at the design meeting with an equipment list and dimensions rather than a room name, and they will get the floor construction, the internal height, the base position and the warranty term written onto the quotation before paying a deposit. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who wants to compare published gym specifications before making contact; anyone with close neighbours who needs an evidenced acoustic figure; anyone who will accept 'built to handle equipment' as a floor specification.

A remote or hybrid worker in Newry, Dundalk, Drogheda, Swords or Dublin working from a kitchen table or a converted bedroom, who wants the working day to end at a door rather than a laptop lid. Their garden is very likely the reason they are looking at an on-site builder rather than a pod: no side access wide enough for a crane, or a plot a lorry cannot reach. They want the room warm enough to use through the winter and finished to a standard they would put a client call in front of, and they are content to specify the size themselves. They will ask for three things before deposit: the electrical schedule, the warranty document, and whether the base is in the price. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who compares on published specification before making contact; anyone who needs a documented U-value to model running cost; anyone outside the north-east or Dublin corridor who has not confirmed coverage.

A beautician, hairdresser, massage therapist, counsellor or maker in Newry, Dundalk, Drogheda, Swords or Dublin who has been renting a room or a chair and wants the overhead gone. They are running a real business, so they think in trading days lost and client impressions made — which is why a two-to-five-day build and a published builder's-finish standard matter to them more than a specification sheet would. They have already taken advice on change of use, and they know whether they need water at the wall. They will get the plumbing provision, the warranty document and the VAT position confirmed in writing before the 10 per cent deposit, and they will visit the Mayobridge showroom to see the finish a client will see. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone assuming the garden-room exemption covers a client-facing business; anyone who needs plumbing confirmed before enquiry; anyone comparing on published price, since none exists.

A family in the north-east or Dublin corridor with a child or adult household member who needs a low-stimulus space to regulate in, and who has probably found that no room in the house can reliably be kept quiet and calm. They are not shopping on price per square metre; they are shopping for a specific set of conditions — acoustic separation, stable temperature, controllable light, a floor that suits the equipment in use. They value that this supplier names the use at all, and that the design can be built around the individual rather than chosen from a catalogue. They will visit the Mayobridge showroom to hear a finished room rather than read about one, and they will ask for the acoustic construction, the insulation build-up and the warranty term in writing before deposit. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who needs an evidenced sound-reduction figure before committing; anyone outside the north-east or Dublin corridor who has not confirmed coverage; anyone expecting the room to be slept in.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE, and building a profile from a range name would be exactly the guess this layer exists to refuse. THE ONE OBSERVATION AVAILABLE: anyone pursuing this record is at the start of a conversation rather than the end of a search. They will be asking the supplier which models the range contains, what each one measures externally, how tall it finishes and what the price includes — and only then will they be in a position to compare it with the documented products in this catalogue. That suits a patient buyer with time to correspond, and suits nobody trying to reach a decision from published information.

A UK homeowner training solo or as a couple, in a garden that has to keep doing other things — a lawn, a patio, an existing shed. Wants a warm, dry room for weights and a mat rather than a full commercial-style setup, and has chosen 12 m2 deliberately because it leaves roughly 18 m2 of the combined allowance for whatever else is on the plot. Prepared to accept a named insulation product without a U-value, and wants the base laid by the same company that builds and wires the room. Will measure internal clear height against the tallest thing they intend to do in it. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, since no Irish route is published; anyone planning a rack plus cardio plus free floor space, for whom the 6 m x 3 m is the honest size; anyone with close neighbours who needs an acoustic specification, which is not published.

A UK homeowner with a suburban back garden who trains at home most days and wants the room warm and dry in January, not just in June. Comfortable spending on the envelope rather than the fit-out, and specifically wants one company to lay the base, build the room and wire it so there is no gap between trades for a defect to fall into. Willing to ask for the warranty in writing rather than assume it, and to measure the internal clear height against the equipment they own before ordering. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, for whom no published route exists from this company; anyone who needs a documented U-value to compare running costs; anyone whose plot already carries a shed or garage, since 15 m2 uses half the 30 m2 combined allowance on its own.

A committed UK home trainer with a reasonably deep back garden who has outgrown a spare room and is replacing a gym membership rather than supplementing one. Owns or intends to own a rack, a bench and at least one cardio machine, so floor area and clear height are the deciding measurements. Wants the room heated and dry through the winter and is willing to accept an unpublished U-value in exchange for a named insulation product. Comfortable with one contractor laying the base and building the room, and has confirmed that 18 m2 still leaves enough of the combined allowance for whatever else stands in the garden. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, since no Irish route is published; anyone on a plot that already carries a garage or large shed; anyone who needs running cost modelled before buying.

A UK remote worker in a terraced house or a small courtyard garden where the plot, not the budget, decides the size. Needs one desk, a chair and a wired connection, and has accepted that nothing else will fit — no storage wall, no second occupant, no meeting space. Wants the room warm enough to use through the winter and is content that the supplier lays the base and wires the room as a single job. Prepared to arrange an electrician separately for the mains run from the house. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, since no Irish route is published; anyone who could fit a larger unit, since the price barely rises with area across this range; anyone who needs the internal dimensions confirmed on paper before committing, as the measurement basis is unstated and the loss to wall build-up is proportionally largest here.

A single UK remote worker in a terraced or small suburban garden where space, not budget, is the binding constraint. Needs a wired, dedicated desk away from the house, plus room for a printer, files or a second monitor — the reason to take this model over the 3 m x 2 m or 2.5 m x 2 m. Values a hard ethernet connection over wifi, wants the room usable through the winter, and prefers one company to handle base, build and wiring rather than coordinating trades. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, since no Irish route is published; anyone who needs to close the door on a second person, as one occupant is the honest capacity; anyone comparing on cost per square metre alone, where this product will not win.

A single remote worker in a terraced or small suburban garden where space, not budget, is the binding constraint. Wants a wired, dedicated desk away from the house and accepts that one person is the honest capacity. Not for gyms, guest rooms or anyone needing to close the door on a second person.

A UK-based photographer, videographer or maker — often working part-time or building a side practice — who needs a room that holds its temperature around equipment and can be used every month of the year. Wants the building, the base and the power under one contract rather than managing a builder and an electrician separately, and is prepared to press the supplier for internal height and wall length before signing because they know a studio lives or dies on those two numbers. Likely to be weighing this against renting studio time. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser, since no Irish route is published; anyone running a client-facing commercial operation from the garden without first checking the incidental-use condition; anyone who needs the room to double as sleeping accommodation, which the NO HUMAN HABITATION condition rules out.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A SMALL GARDEN THAT NEEDS A ROOM AND A PLACE FOR THE TOOLS. Combining both into one compact building with a sheltered strip in front is sensible planning on a tight plot, and 8.35 m2 of stated internal floor is enough for a desk, a chair and a bookcase. THEY ARE BUYING A SHELL and should treat the insulation and roof covering as separate, priced decisions. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs a reliable external footprint from the website; nor for one comparing the headline price against a turnkey insulated room.

A GARDENER RATHER THAN A REMOTE WORKER. Somebody with tools, pots and a mower who also wants a dry, pleasant space to sit or pot up in — the two-room layout is designed for exactly that, and the manufacturer's stated use is storage. THEY WILL BE SELF-BUILDING on their own base. NOT FOR: a home office, where the split layout and the 28 mm walls both work against it; nor for a buyer who needs the usable room size confirmed before ordering.

A homeowner whose garden or access route genuinely cannot accommodate a larger unit, but who still wants a delivered, factory-finished steel cabin with a 50-year warranty. Budgeting roughly EUR 37k-47k once VAT, base and connections are added. Anyone without a hard site constraint should look at the 19m² Studio first.

An Irish homeowner with roughly EUR 35k-45k available once VAT, base and connections are counted, who wants the project handled rather than managed. Buying a studio, large home office or garden lounge and prioritising delivered-finished convenience and a very long warranty over cost per square metre.

A homeowner who needs plumbing in the garden building — a shower room, WC or kitchenette — and is therefore not really comparing it against the dry studios in the range. Budgeting roughly EUR 57k-67k once VAT, base and connections are added. Anyone who does not need water should look hard at the 26m² Studio instead.

An Irish homeowner with roughly EUR 45k-55k available once VAT, base and connections are counted, who wants a substantial delivered studio without managing a build. Suits a large home office, garden lounge or studio in daily year-round use, and someone who has compared the range and spotted that this is where the value sits.

A homeowner for whom finish quality and brand tier matter more than cost per square metre, budgeting roughly EUR 63k-73k once VAT, base and connections are added. Comfortable paying a premium for the top specification, but should still ask precisely what that premium buys.

An Irish homeowner creating independent accommodation for an adult child or ageing parent, with good site access and roughly EUR 85k-95k available once VAT, base, craneage and connections are counted. Wants the building to arrive finished and habitable rather than to run a construction project, and is prepared to handle planning and a services connection.

An Irish homeowner around EUR 19k-24k all-in who has already decided on Concept Modular and is choosing between its two office tiers. Values a delivered, factory-finished, maintenance-free steel building and a warranty that outlasts any mortgage.

An Irish homeowner budgeting around EUR 17k-22k once VAT and mains connection are added, who wants a factory-finished office delivered rather than a kit to build, and who is buying for the long term. Suits someone who has been put off by timber maintenance and wants a steel structure they will never re-treat.

SOMEONE ATTRACTED BY A NAME RATHER THAN A SPECIFICATION. 'Concept' suggests something designed and distinctive, and for a buyer who has seen the product in person that may be exactly right — but the catalogue offers nothing to confirm it, which makes this the Bertilo record most dependent on a showroom visit or a detailed enquiry. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published and no showroom is reachable; nor for anyone comparing products on paper, where this record has the least to compare.

SOMEONE WHO HAS PAINTED A TIMBER SHED ONCE TOO OFTEN. Maintenance is the motivation, and a modern clad exterior on a general-purpose building lets them decide the use later while removing the annual job. THEY ARE PRACTICAL RATHER THAN DESIGN-LED, though the contemporary form suits a modern house. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants the supplier to have solved the interior, where the office and pod configurations exist; nor for anyone comparing on published specification, since neither the material nor the size is described.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A LOW-MAINTENANCE CONTEMPORARY OFFICE AND HAS NOTICED THE MATERIAL DESIGNATION. They are shopping on finish as much as on size — a modern-looking building that will not need painting — and the ALU suffix is what drew them to this record rather than its timber siblings. THEY WILL WANT THE MATERIAL DETAIL, which is exactly what is missing. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing on floor area or price, where nothing here can be compared; nor for a business receiving clients, where the incidental-use condition becomes live.

A SINGLE HOME WORKER WITH A SMALL GARDEN. One desk, a door that closes, and a building small enough not to dominate the lawn or the allowance — the most common garden-office requirement there is. THEY WANT SOMETHING THAT LOOKS CONTEMPORARY and arrives ready to use. THE THERMAL QUESTION IS THEIR REAL ONE, since a small pod used five days a week is only as good as its insulation. NOT FOR: two people or equipment, where the larger office models exist; nor for a buyer needing a published specification before enquiring.

A HOUSEHOLD CHOOSING A MODERN ROOM FROM A LARGE EUROPEAN CATALOGUE ON PRICE AND APPEARANCE. They have shortlisted several similar models and expect the supplier to fill in the specification — which, for Hansa24, is the right expectation: the figures exist, they are simply not in Atlas. THEY SHOULD ASK BY SKU RATHER THAN BY NAME, because the certified layers record letters and names being reused across different buildings. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the exemption demonstrated from published information before making contact.

SOMEONE BUYING THEIR FIRST GARDEN ROOM AND SHOPPING ON APPEARANCE. A modern building, an ordinary size, a recognisable supplier with a lot of models — which describes a large share of the market. THEY HAVE NOT YET THOUGHT ABOUT THE HEIGHT LIMIT, which on a flat-roofed contemporary building is the condition most likely to catch them out. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the exemption demonstrated before ordering; nor for a period house, where the range's traditional forms sit more comfortably.

SOMEONE MAKING USE OF A CORNER THEY CANNOT OTHERWISE USE. A rectangular garden usually has one awkward corner, and a corner-plan building turns it into the most sheltered spot on the plot — with a veranda facing back across the lawn. THEY ARE BUYING FOR THE PLAN SHAPE, not for square metres, and at a published 18 m2 they have roughly 12 m2 of the allowance left over for a shed. NOT FOR: a household that also wants a large existing structure kept and a veranda counted, where the arithmetic tightens; nor for anyone who will not check which building the SKU refers to.

A homeowner with an awkward garden corner to use, wanting a plain square room of about 12 m2, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 6,240 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE ADDING A WELLNESS FEATURE RATHER THAN SOLVING A SPACE PROBLEM. They already have the house they need; this is a discretionary purchase for recovery, relaxation or cold-water bathing, and they are buying from an Irish showroom where they can see the build. THEY ARE ALSO, OFTEN, THE SAME HOUSEHOLD THAT WILL WANT A GARDEN OFFICE LATER — which is why the allowance arithmetic matters to them more than the sauna's own modest size suggests. NOT FOR: anyone whose garden allowance is already committed, or who assumes small structures do not count.

A HOME WORKER WHO WANTS THE SUPPLIER TO HAVE SOLVED THE INTERIOR, not just delivered a shell. They expect an office-ready building — layout, glazing, somewhere for power — and are willing to pay for a configuration rather than fit one out themselves. THE QUESTIONS THEY MOST NEED ANSWERED ARE THERMAL, since a daily workspace lives or dies on its envelope and nothing is published. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a business with client visits, where the incidental-use condition becomes live.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT ALREADY HAS A POOL AND IS TIRED OF WET FLOORS INDOORS. Changing space, towels, pool equipment and somewhere to sit out of the sun — a specific, practical requirement, and one that arrives after the larger investment has already been made. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN BY DEFINITION, which eases the allowance question, though it does not remove it. NOT FOR: a household without a pool, where the base Cubus 2 or the Office configuration is the sensible choice; nor for an Irish buyer, on availability grounds.

TWO PEOPLE WORKING FROM HOME, OR ONE PERSON WITH EQUIPMENT. A room that has to hold two desks, or a desk plus storage, printing and materials — the requirement that justifies the top of an office line rather than the middle. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN AND A DAILY, YEAR-ROUND USE PATTERN, which makes the missing thermal specification the most consequential gap for them. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a small garden, where the largest undimensioned model is the least defensible option.

A FAMILY WITH A POOL AND SEVERAL PEOPLE USING IT AT ONCE. Children, visitors, towels and equipment — the reason a larger poolhouse exists, and a requirement the smaller model would frustrate. THEY HAVE THE GARDEN FOR IT, but are also the household most likely to have already used part of the allowance on other structures, which is the arithmetic that matters here. NOT FOR: a small pool or a couple, where the Cubus 2 Poolhouse is proportionate; nor for an Irish buyer, on availability grounds.

SOMEONE AT THE SHORTLIST STAGE RATHER THAN THE ORDER STAGE. The record is useful for establishing that a 4 × 4 m DREUX exists and is comfortably exempt; it is not useful for choosing between specifications or comparing prices. THEY SHOULD MOVE TO THE 44 mm OR 66 mm RECORD once they know whether they want a summer room or a warmer shell. NOT FOR: anyone at the point of ordering, where the wall class must be named on the quotation.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING A SUMMER ROOM AND KNOWING IT. A studio, a hobby space, a spring-to-autumn office, a garden sitting room — uses where a 44 mm log cabin is exactly right and an insulated build would be money spent on a season they will not use it in. THEY ARE OFTEN SELF-BUILDING, given the kit pricing and the modest size. NOT FOR: daily winter working, where the insulated classes are the honest option; nor for a buyer who expects to retrofit insulation to this specification later.

SOMEONE WHO CARES HOW THE BUILDING FEELS AND IS NOT PLANNING TO SIT IN IT IN JANUARY. A thick-walled small cabin makes a good studio, workshop or garden room, and the extra timber shows in the door, the corners and the sound it keeps out. THEY ARE USUALLY UPGRADING FROM A SHED rather than replacing a room in the house. NOT FOR: a daily winter workspace, where the insulated classes are the correct product; nor for a buyer for whom the 66 mm premium is better spent on insulation.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A CLEAR GARDEN THAT WANTS THE BIGGEST ROOM IT CAN HAVE WITHOUT A PLANNING APPLICATION. That is a common and sensible brief, and 25 m2 is close to the practical ceiling for it. THEY ARE USUALLY BUYING FOR SPRING-TO-AUTUMN USE, or intend to heat the room themselves, since the specification is uninsulated. THEY ARE OFTEN SELF-BUILDING or using a local builder, given the kit pricing. NOT FOR: a plot that already carries structures; nor for daily winter working without upgrading to an insulated class.

SOMEONE BUYING ONCE AND BUYING WELL, WITHIN THE EXEMPTION. They want the largest and most solid building they can have without involving a planning authority, and they are prepared to add heating and their own insulation later or accept seasonal use. A MUSIC ROOM OR STUDIO SUITS THE HEAVIER WALL, which does more for sound than for heat. NOT FOR: a plot that already carries structures, where 5 m2 of margin will not survive; nor for a buyer who reads 66 mm as year-round capability.

NOBODY SHOULD BE BUYING FROM THIS RECORD IN ITS CURRENT STATE. THE RECORD'S VALUE IS AS A REMINDER that a catalogue entry can look complete and still not identify a product. NOT FOR: any buyer, until the attribution is resolved — and in any case not for anyone seeking exempt development, since the footprint rules that out.

SOMEONE BUILDING A WORKSHOP, STUDIO OR GYM RATHER THAN AN OFFICE, ON A LARGE PLOT, WHO IS PREPARED TO MAKE A PLANNING APPLICATION. That is a different kind of project from a garden room, and it should be approached as one — with a base, a professional drawing and a timeline. THREE-SEASON USE SUITS A WORKSHOP better than it suits daily desk work. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants an exempt garden office; nor for year-round working without an insulated specification.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS THE BUILDING TO FEEL SOLID AND IS NOT PRIMARILY BUYING WARMTH. A 66 mm log room reads as a proper structure rather than a shed, which matters to buyers who will look at it for twenty years — and they accept both the planning application and the three-season limitation that come with it. THEY OFTEN HAVE A WORKSHOP OR STUDIO USE IN MIND. NOT FOR: a homeowner assuming thicker walls mean winter use; nor for anyone who needs to stay inside the exemption.

A FAMILY BUYING A SECOND LIVING SPACE WITH SOMEWHERE TO SIT OUTSIDE IT, ON A CLEAR PLOT. The covered terrace is the reason to choose this over the RAMSAY, and it suits a household that will use the garden around the building as much as the room itself. THEY MUST HAVE AN OTHERWISE EMPTY BACK GARDEN, because 28.91 m2 leaves almost nothing. THEY SHOULD ALSO BE BUDGETING FOR INSULATION on top of the headline price. NOT FOR: a plot with an existing shed; nor for a buyer assessing the building on its indoor figure alone.

A HOUSEHOLD BUILDING AN OUTDOOR ROOM RATHER THAN AN INDOOR ONE, ON A LARGE PLOT, AND PREPARED TO APPLY FOR PERMISSION. The covered area is the product here — somewhere to sit out in Irish weather with an enclosed room attached — and that is a real brief that most garden-room catalogues do not serve. THEY ARE SELF-BUILDING and will already understand this is a planning application, not an exempt purchase. NOT FOR: a homeowner wanting an exempt garden office; nor for anyone reading the 19.01 m2 floor as the size of the building.

A UK HOUSEHOLD WITH A NARROW GARDEN AND ONE THING TO PUT IN IT. Where a squarer building would dominate or simply not fit, a 5.5 × 2.5 m room along the boundary gives full length and leaves the lawn intact — with more than half the allowance still free. THEY WILL USE IT FOR ONE PURPOSE, most often a desk, and they will build it themselves. NOT FOR: a household wanting two uses in one room, where the depth defeats them; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

SOMEONE WHO WILL USE THE GARDEN AROUND THE BUILDING, NOT JUST THE ROOM. The canopy is bought for the shoulder seasons — a covered step, a place to put a chair, somewhere to shelter while unlocking the door — and those small things decide whether a garden room gets used from March to October. THEY ARE A UK SELF-BUILDER. NOT FOR: a buyer keeping the roofed footprint to an absolute minimum, where the canopy works against the allowance; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

A UK HOUSEHOLD WITH A SMALL GARDEN, ONE OCCUPANT AND NO APPETITE FOR MAINTENANCE. Composite cladding on a compact pod is bought precisely so that it can be forgotten about, and a pent roof keeps the profile low against a boundary. THEY WILL BUILD IT THEMSELVES over a weekend or two. NOT FOR: anyone needing storage, a second person or equipment depth; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

A UK SELF-BUILDER WHO WANTS A LARGE, LOW-MAINTENANCE ROOM AND WILL NOT BE RE-TREATING TIMBER. Composite cladding on a 26 m2 building removes a lot of future work, and the Huntly factory line means the panels are the supplier's own product rather than a bought-in finish. THEY WILL BE ERECTING IT THEMSELVES or hiring locally. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published; nor for a garden with existing structures, where the margin disappears.

SOMEONE FURNISHING A SMALL ROOM PROPERLY. A dwarf wall gives somewhere to put a desk against, run a cable behind and hang a radiator on, while keeping the light — which is exactly the compromise most single-occupant offices actually need. THEY HAVE THOUGHT ABOUT THE LAYOUT, not just the size. NOT FOR: a buyer wanting maximum glass or maximum wall, where the Glazed and Solid variants are the clearer choices; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

SOMEONE WHO WILL SIT IN A SMALL ROOM FOR HOURS AND WANTS IT TO FEEL LIGHT. On 8.75 m2 the glazing is what stops the building feeling like a box, and for a single-occupant office facing a pleasant garden that matters more than any other option on the list. THEY WILL BUILD IT THEMSELVES and will want a south or west aspect. NOT FOR: a workshop or studio needing wall space, where the Solid variant is the correct product; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

A UK HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A LIGHT ROOM AND WILL BUILD IT THEMSELVES. Fifteen and a half square metres with generous glazing makes a pleasant place to work, and the DIY route with pictorial instructions and video tutorials is what brings an insulated double-glazed room into reach at this price. THEY WILL WANT A SOUTH OR WEST ASPECT. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer without a confirmed route; nor for a north-facing or exposed position, where the extra glazing on a 0.7 W/m2K envelope works against them.

A UK HOUSEHOLD BUYING ITS FIRST GARDEN OFFICE ON A MODEST BUDGET, AND BUILDING IT THEMSELVES. Under nine square metres, insulated, double glazed, with more than twenty of allowance to spare — there is very little that can go wrong here except the build, and Dunster House supports that with instructions, videos and assembly help. THEY HAVE A SMALL GARDEN AND ONE PERSON TO ACCOMMODATE. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published; nor for anyone needing storage or a second occupant.

A UK HOUSEHOLD ADDING A FIRST GARDEN OFFICE WITHOUT WANTING A PROJECT. Eleven square metres, insulated, double glazed, with nearly nineteen of allowance left over — that removes almost every risk from the purchase except the build itself, and Dunster House supports the build with pictorial instructions, video tutorials and assembly help. THEY ARE COMFORTABLE WITH A WEEKEND OR TWO OF WORK. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer without a confirmed route; nor for a household needing two uses in one room, where 2.5 m of depth defeats them.

A UK HOUSEHOLD WITH A NARROW GARDEN AND SOMETHING PRACTICAL TO DO IN THE ROOM. Solid walls on a long, shallow plan give bench, shelf and board space that a glazed model cannot — a workshop, a hobby room, a studio — and the pressure-treated timber suits a building that will take knocks. THEY WILL ERECT IT THEMSELVES or hire locally. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a light, outward-facing room, where the Glazed variants exist; nor for an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

A UK HOUSEHOLD BUYING A PROPER WORKING ROOM AND DOING THE BUILD THEMSELVES. Nineteen square metres, insulated, double glazed, with eleven square metres of allowance left over — that is a complete answer for most home-office briefs, and the DIY route is what makes it affordable. THEY ARE COMPETENT OR HAVE A BUILDER, and they will lay their own base. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer without a confirmed delivery route; nor for anyone expecting the supplier to install it — Dunster House never does.

A CAPABLE SELF-BUILDER WITH A LARGE EMPTY GARDEN, IN THE UNITED KINGDOM. Dunster House designs for the DIY market and supports it properly — pictorial instructions, video tutorials, assembly support — so a buyer who will erect it themselves or hire a local builder gets an insulated 26 m2 room for a shell price. THEY WILL HAVE ARRANGED THE BASE THEMSELVES. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer, since no Irish delivery is published; nor for a plot already carrying a shed, where 3.75 m2 of margin will not survive.

SOMEONE WHOSE REQUIREMENT GENUINELY EXCEEDS WHAT EXEMPTED DEVELOPMENT ALLOWS, AND WHO KNOWS IT. A large studio, a workshop, a room for several people at once — and a willingness to budget for drawings, fees and a planning timeline. THAT IS A LEGITIMATE POSITION; the failure mode is arriving at it by accident. THE BUYER MOST AT RISK is the one who walks into a Wicklow, Cork or Wexford showroom, sees a garden room, and assumes the category name settles the planning question. NOT FOR: anyone relying on the exemption, at any garden size — the product is over the limit on its own published figures.

A homeowner in Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare or Wexford with a modest garden — or one that already carries a shed — who needs a single quiet, warm room for one person: a desk, a hobby bench, a reading room. They are choosing this size to protect the rest of the garden and the rest of the planning allowance, not because it is the cheapest thing available, and they care that the small building is built to the same standard as the large ones. They understand that the advertised EUR 6,200 is a materials figure, that a concrete base is required regardless of size, and that the proportional cost of finishing is highest on the smallest unit. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the four published counties; anyone who needs to close the door on two people, since at 9 m2 nominal the working room is smaller still; anyone comparing on headline price without asking for the Full Turnkey figure.

A homeowner in Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare or Wexford with a garden that has to do two jobs at once — somewhere to work or sit, and somewhere to put the mower, bikes and garden tools — and who has realised that a separate shed would take a second bite out of the same 30 m2 allowance. They are prioritising planning efficiency and site tidiness over maximum room size, and they accept that the living space is meaningfully smaller than the 18 m2 headline. They will ask for the room dimension and the store dimension separately before ordering, and for the Full Turnkey Price broken down by section, since the two halves need different finishes. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the four published counties; anyone who wants maximum usable room area for the planning cost, for whom a single-volume model of the same nominal size gives more; anyone who needs a published warranty.

An Irish homeowner working to roughly EUR 10k-20k who wants a durable, low-upkeep room and holds a realistic view of groundworks. Suits either a competent self-finisher who takes the basic unit and fits out themselves, or someone who wants a single contract covering everything. Not for anyone expecting the entry price to be the final price.

A homeowner in Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare or Wexford who wants one properly built, year-round room — an office, a studio, a hobby space — and who is deliberately not maximising the footprint, either because the garden still has to function or because a shed is already standing. They value a durable, low-upkeep exterior over a timber building needing annual treatment, and they hold a realistic view of groundworks: a concrete base is a construction requirement here, not an optional extra. They are choosing consciously between finishing the basic unit themselves and buying the full turnkey package, and they will get both figures in writing. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the four published counties, who has no route to this product; anyone expecting the advertised figure to be the final price; anyone who needs a published warranty term or a U-value before committing.

A homeowner in Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare or Wexford with a reasonably empty back garden who wants a proper room rather than a shed — a family space, a large office, a studio — and who has done the arithmetic on the combined allowance before choosing the size. They are comfortable with a site-survey-and-build process rather than a delivered pod, and they are making a conscious choice between taking the basic unit and finishing it themselves or buying the full turnkey package. They will get the Full Turnkey Price in writing, because on a building this size the gap between the tiers is at its widest, and they will establish who warrants the base and who warrants the building. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the four published counties; anyone whose plot already carries a garage or large shed, since only 6 m2 of headroom remains; anyone who needs a published warranty term before committing.

A homeowner in Dublin, Wicklow, Kildare or Wexford with a clear back garden and a genuine need for a large single room — a studio, a family space, a home office with a seating area — who has checked that nothing else on the plot eats into the 30 m2 combined allowance. They are comfortable managing a project rather than buying a finished product: a site survey, a substantial concrete base, and a deliberate choice between the materials tier and the full turnkey tier. They value low-maintenance fibre cement over timber that needs annual treatment, and they will ask for the U-value in writing because the supplier's claim of insulation 'to the same standard as the main house' invites the question. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the four published counties, who has no route to this product at all; anyone whose garden already carries a shed or garage; anyone who needs a published warranty before signing.

A HYBRID WORKER WITH A SMALL GARDEN AND A SINGLE REQUIREMENT. One desk, one occupant, and a preference for keeping most of the lawn — with the added comfort of buying from an Irish supplier whose published size lets them check the exemption themselves before enquiring. THEY ALSO HAVE THE MOST HEADROOM IN THE RANGE, 21 m2, which matters if a shed or a future garden store is in prospect. NOT FOR: two occupants, a gym, or anyone storing equipment as well as working — the 4.0 m × 3.0 m at 12 m2 is the honest next step up.

SOMEONE WORKING FROM HOME MOST DAYS WHO WANTS THE DECISION TO BE UNCOMPLICATED. They need a proper desk, a door that closes and somewhere to put a printer and a filing box — not a studio. The published size lets them satisfy themselves on area before speaking to anyone, and the supplier being Irish means installation and support are local. THEIR ONE REMAINING QUESTION IS HEIGHT, and it is worth asking early. NOT FOR: a household needing the room to double as a gym or guest space — that requires 4 m of depth, which starts at the 4.0 m × 4.0 m model.

A HOUSEHOLD WHERE THE ROOM HAS TO SERVE MORE THAN ONE PERSON OR MORE THAN ONE PURPOSE. Two people working on alternate days, or an office that becomes a gym at six o'clock — the uses that need floor in front of the furniture rather than only alongside it. They have a garden wide enough to take a 4 m depth and still leave the required open space. NOT FOR: a narrow plot, where the 5.0 m × 3.0 m at 15 m2 fits the shape better; nor for a garden already carrying a garage, where 14 m2 of remaining allowance may not be enough.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A NARROW GARDEN AND A REAL WORKSPACE REQUIREMENT. The 3 m depth suits a plot where width is the scarce dimension, and the 5 m length gives room for more than a desk — a common Irish suburban shape. They are comfortable buying from a published size list and want the supplier close enough to visit. THEY HAVE HALF THE ALLOWANCE LEFT, which is the right position for a household that may add a shed later. NOT FOR: a room that must work in two directions at once — the 4.0 m × 4.0 m or 5.0 m × 4.0 m models exist for that.

A HOUSEHOLD TREATING THE GARDEN ROOM AS A PERMANENT EXTENSION OF THE HOUSE. Two working adults, or a workspace that also serves as a gym and an occasional family room — the requirement that justifies committing two thirds of the allowance to one building. They have a reasonably large, otherwise clear garden and they intend this to be the only structure in it. NOT FOR: a household that also wants a shed, where 10 m2 of remaining allowance disappears quickly; nor for a small garden, where the 25 m2 private open space condition may bind before the building allowance does.

SOMEONE WHOSE GARDEN DICTATES THE SHAPE OF THE BUILDING. A long narrow plot, a boundary run, or a site where a deeper structure would block light or a path — the geometry decides before the specification does. They want maximum accommodation without the building dominating the garden, and they are working from published dimensions with an Irish supplier. NOT FOR: a household whose requirement is really about depth — a gym, a studio, two simultaneous desks — where the 4.0 m × 4.0 m or 5.0 m × 4.0 m models do more with the same or less area.

A HOUSEHOLD MAKING ONE LARGE COMMITMENT RATHER THAN SEVERAL SMALL ONES. They have a big garden, no shed worth keeping, and a requirement that genuinely needs 24 m2 — a studio, a workshop, or a room serving several members of the family. THEY UNDERSTAND THAT THIS BUILDING IS EFFECTIVELY THEIR WHOLE ALLOWANCE, and they are content for it to be the only structure in the garden. NOT FOR: anyone with an existing shed, garage or greenhouse of any size; nor for a household that expects to add storage later, since there will be no allowance left to do it with.

A homeowner with a small or already-occupied garden who wants a properly insulated room delivered and built rather than a kit to assemble, is comfortable arranging an electrician separately, and is budgeting from EUR 14,280 inclusive of VAT with fitting included and decoration and power still to come.

A homeowner with a shallow garden wanting a compact insulated office delivered and built rather than self-assembled, comfortable arranging an electrician separately, budgeting from EUR 16,380 inclusive of VAT with fitting included and decoration and power still to come.

A homeowner with a long, shallow garden wanting an insulated working room built for them, comfortable arranging an electrician separately, budgeting from EUR 19,630 inclusive of VAT with fitting included and decoration and power still to come.

SOMEONE WITH A PERIOD OR TRADITIONAL HOUSE WHO WANTS THE GARDEN BUILDING TO MATCH IT. A cube in the back garden of a nineteenth-century terrace looks wrong to many people, and the place-named houses exist for exactly that objection. THEY ARE CHOOSING ON CHARACTER, which is legitimate — and which makes the roof-covering question the one piece of technical detail they most need. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a contemporary house, where the Cubo, Cubus and Pentus lines are the intended answer.

SOMEONE SOLVING TWO PROBLEMS AT ONCE — a garden room and the storage or shelter that usually follows it. Buying both together avoids mismatched materials and a second delivery, which is why packaged sets appeal. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST AT RISK OF UNDER-COUNTING THEIR ALLOWANCE, because the second element rarely registers as a building. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a garden already close to its limit, where adding two structures at once is the least advisable move.

A BUYER WHO HAS SEEN THE BUILDING IN PERSON. That is the honest characterisation: with no dimensions, no roof form and no specification published, a purchase decision here can only follow a showroom visit or a detailed conversation. FOR A CONTINENTAL BUYER WITH ACCESS TO BOTH, the plain Concept may be exactly the right shell to fit out. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, who has neither the showroom nor the purchasing route; nor for anyone shortlisting products from published information, where this record offers the least of any in the catalogue.

REALISTICALLY, A CONTINENTAL BUYER RATHER THAN AN IRISH ONE. Bertilo's range is sold into markets its Estonian shipping actually reaches, and for a homeowner there this is a mainstream, well-established garden building. FOR AN IRISH READER THE USEFUL FUNCTION OF THIS RECORD IS DIFFERENT: it explains why a product that appears in searches cannot presently be bought here, and what would have to change. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner wanting a delivered, installed garden room; nor for anyone who needs to demonstrate exemption compliance, since no area or height is published.

SOMEONE CHOOSING A MODEL NUMBER FROM A RANGE, WHICH IS EXACTLY THE DECISION THIS CATALOGUE CANNOT HELP WITH. They have settled on the Cubo form and are now picking between 1, 2 and 3 — and will find that the numerals are names rather than sizes. THE HONEST ADVICE IS TO GET A DRAWING PER MODEL. FOR AN IRISH READER, the prior question remains availability: Estonia-only shipping with no Irish distributor. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner needing a delivered product; nor for a buyer who expects the model number to indicate floor area.

SOMEONE BUYING GARDEN LEISURE RATHER THAN GARDEN WORKSPACE. A place to sit, read and look at the garden — which is a legitimate brief and one most of this catalogue's records are not designed around. THEY ARE LESS LIKELY THAN AN OFFICE BUYER TO THINK ABOUT PLANNING AT ALL, which is why the allowance and the no-habitation condition are worth putting in front of them explicitly. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner on availability grounds; nor for anyone intending guest sleeping use, which the exemption excludes.

A BUYER WHO WANTS THE LARGEST VERSION OF A FORM THEY HAVE ALREADY CHOSEN. In most ranges that is a straightforward upgrade; here it is an act of faith, because nothing published confirms that the Cubo 3 is larger than the Cubo 1. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER WITH THE MOST TO LOSE if the building turns out to approach the allowance on a garden that already holds a shed. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for anyone relying on the exemption without a measured footprint.

A HOUSEHOLD WANTING A GENEROUS GARDEN SITTING ROOM — space for several people, and a configuration built around comfort rather than work. They are buying the upper end of a range and will expect the specification to justify it, which is exactly what the published evidence cannot do. THEY SHOULD TREAT THE ENQUIRY AS THE SPECIFICATION EXERCISE, not the catalogue. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on availability grounds; nor for a small garden, where an undimensioned building at the top of a range is the riskiest possible choice.

SOMEONE ENTERING A LARGE RANGE AT ITS MOST ACCESSIBLE POINT. A first garden building, a modest requirement, and a preference for a manufacturer with variants to grow into later — which the Cubus line, with its Lounge, Office and Poolhouse configurations, provides more than any other Bertilo family. THEY WILL BE COMPARING MODEL NAMES ACROSS TWO SIMILARLY NAMED LINES and should be careful about which they are quoting. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published; nor for a buyer who needs a confirmed size before enquiring.

A BUYER WHO WANTS A PLAIN, ADAPTABLE GARDEN BUILDING RATHER THAN A CONFIGURED ONE. They intend to fit it out themselves, or their use is mixed enough that no single configuration fits — which makes the base model the sensible choice and avoids paying for a designation the catalogue cannot define. THEY STILL NEED THE FOOTPRINT AND HEIGHT IN WRITING. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner on availability grounds; nor for anyone who wants the supplier to have solved the interior layout for them, where the Office or Lounge variants are the intended answer.

A COUPLE OR FAMILY WANTING A SECOND SITTING ROOM AT THE END OF THE GARDEN. Somewhere to read, watch the garden or escape a busy house — used in daylight, not overnight, which is what keeps the exemption available to them. They value a configured product over a bare shell. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on availability grounds; nor for a household that will inevitably put guests in it, since that is a different consent route; nor for anyone needing a workspace, which the Office configuration addresses.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A LARGE GARDEN AND A REQUIREMENT FOR MORE THAN ONE ROOM'S WORTH OF SPACE. They are choosing the top of a range on the reasonable assumption that it is the biggest — and they are the buyer who most needs to know that assumption is unverified. THEY WILL ALSO BE THE ONE MOST EXPOSED to the combined-allowance arithmetic if the garden is not empty. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a small garden, where an undimensioned large building is the least defensible choice.

A FAMILY WANTING A SECOND LIVING ROOM IN THE GARDEN, USED BY SEVERAL PEOPLE AT ONCE. Space to sit, entertain and spread out — the requirement that pushes a buyer to the top of a range and into the leisure configuration. THEY ARE SPENDING AT THE UPPER END and should expect the specification to justify it; the catalogue cannot, so the enquiry must. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner on availability grounds; nor for a garden with existing structures, where the largest undimensioned model is the least defensible choice; nor for guest accommodation.

THEY WILL WANT THE MATERIAL DETAIL, which is exactly what the catalogue lacks. A LOW-MAINTENANCE BUYER WHO NEEDS MORE ROOM THAN THE FIRST MODEL OFFERS — or believes they do, since the numeral does not confirm it. THEY SHOULD ASK FOR BOTH MODELS' FOOTPRINTS SIDE BY SIDE rather than assuming the numbering is a ladder. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for anyone comparing on published specification, where this line has none.

A homeowner with a large garden able to accommodate a 43 m2 structure, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting a covered outdoor entertaining space as the primary purpose with a substantial room attached, and budgeting around EUR 16,450 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

An established garden, a period property, or a neighbour whose outlook matters — the cases where appearance is not a preference but a constraint. THEY ARE CHOOSING BETWEEN TWO TRADITIONAL MODELS THE CATALOGUE CANNOT SEPARATE, so the decision will come down to photographs and a conversation. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for a buyer who needs the specification settled before making contact.

SOMEONE AT THE BEGINNING OF THE PROCESS RATHER THAN THE END. They know they want a garden building and are looking at a broad range without having settled on a size, a use or a finish — which is exactly who a plain named model suits. THEY SHOULD EXPECT THE FIRST SUPPLIER CONVERSATION TO BE ABOUT DIMENSIONS, since the catalogue offers no starting figure. NOT FOR: a buyer with a specific brief — an office, a gym, a poolhouse — where the configured models in the same range are the better entry point.

SOMEONE WANTING A MODERN-LOOKING GARDEN BUILDING AT THE SMALLER END OF A RANGE. The pent roof suits a contemporary house and a tight boundary, and the entry numeral suits a first purchase or a modest requirement. THEY START WITH ONE PIECE OF PLANNING CERTAINTY — the 3 m limit — which is more than buyers of the Cubo and Cubus lines get from the name alone. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published; nor for anyone needing extra internal height, where only a tiled or slated pitched roof would raise the limit to 4 m.

A BUYER WITH A CONTEMPORARY HOUSE AND A BOUNDARY TO RESPECT. The pent roof is chosen for how the building sits — low toward the neighbour, taller toward the garden — and the mid numeral for a workable size without going to the top of the range. THEY HAVE A CHOICE OF FOUR CONFIGURATIONS, which suits a household still deciding what the room is for. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for anyone needing internal height, since the pent form caps them at 3 m by design.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A BRIGHT ROOM FACING THE GARDEN AND A LOW PROFILE FACING THE NEIGHBOUR. That is the pent-roofed lounge in one sentence, and it describes a large share of Irish suburban gardens — which makes the availability position the frustrating part. THEY ARE BUYING FOR LIGHT AND OUTLOOK rather than for square metres. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on availability grounds; nor for a workspace, where the Office configuration is intended; nor for guest sleeping, which the exemption excludes.

A HOUSEHOLD WANTING A LARGE CONTEMPORARY GARDEN BUILDING ON A SITE WHERE PROFILE MATTERS. A wide pent-roofed room, low toward the boundary, glazed toward the garden — an architectural choice as much as a practical one. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO MEET THE 3 m LIMIT, because a bigger building under a mono-pitch is a taller one. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a garden already holding structures, where the largest undimensioned model is the least defensible choice.

A FAMILY WANTING A LARGE, LIGHT GARDEN ROOM TO SIT AND ENTERTAIN IN. Space for several people, a wall of glazing toward the garden, and a building that does not loom over the boundary — the brief that this configuration is designed for. THEY ARE COMMITTING SERIOUS BUDGET at the top of a range whose specifications are unpublished, which is the imbalance to correct before ordering. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a garden already carrying structures; nor for guest accommodation, which is a different consent route.

A homeowner with a long boundary run and no other outbuildings, wanting to consolidate room, storage and covered seating into one structure, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 9,050 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WHOSE LAST GARDEN ROOM ENDED UP FULL OF LAWNMOWERS. That is the specific failure this layout prevents: a separate lockable store means the room stays a room. THEY HAVE ONE PLACE IN THE GARDEN THEY WANT TO BUILD and would rather put everything there than scatter structures around the plot. NOT FOR: a household that already owns a shed worth keeping, where the plain house is the better use of the allowance; nor for a garden close to 30 m2, where two roofed elements are the least likely combination to fit.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A TIMBER BUILDING THAT LOOKS CONTEMPORARY RATHER THAN RUSTIC. The pent roof and a timber finish is a common and successful combination — modern lines, natural material — and it suits both a period house and a new one. THEY ARE ALSO A BUYER WHO READS PRODUCT NAMES CAREFULLY, which this range rewards less often than it should. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for anyone unwilling to maintain a timber exterior, where the HPL cladding line or Adman's steel is the better direction.

A homeowner who needs a large garden room with washing facilities but not overnight accommodation, who can reach mains water and foul drainage at the chosen position, is prepared to commission a plumber and electrician separately, has few other outbuildings, and is budgeting around EUR 13,180 for the delivered kit before groundworks and connections.

SOMEONE FOR WHOM THE GARDEN BUILDING IS PART OF THE GARDEN'S DESIGN. They want an object worth looking at from the house, not a shed with better windows — a legitimate and under-served brief, and the reason a line called Modern Art exists at all. THEY ARE BUYING ON APPEARANCE, which makes the unpublished height the risk they are least likely to anticipate. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a workspace, where the Office configurations are intended; nor for overnight use.

A DESIGN-CONSCIOUS BUYER WHO HAS ALREADY DECIDED ON THE LINE AND IS NOW CHOOSING BETWEEN TWO MODELS. That is the decision this record exists to be honest about: the catalogue cannot separate them, so the comparison has to be made from the supplier's own drawings. THEY ARE SPENDING ON APPEARANCE and will accept a longer conversation to get the right one. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a buyer whose priority is a defensible exemption position, where a dimensioned Irish product is the sounder choice.

A HOUSEHOLD PROVIDING A HOME FOR ONE PERSON — an adult child staying local, or a parent moving closer. They are commissioning a small dwelling, not buying a garden building, and their decision turns on occupancy, services and consent rather than on square metres per pound. THEY MUST BUDGET FOR PROCESS: drainage, heating, fire safety and a planning route are all in scope. NOT FOR: a workspace buyer, or anyone outside the supplier's South East England service area.

A SOUTH EAST ENGLAND FAMILY CREATING INDEPENDENT ACCOMMODATION — typically for an adult child or an ageing parent who needs proximity without sharing the house. The driver is occupancy, and the building follows. They must accept a heavier process than a garden-office buyer: services, drainage, fire and building standards, and a consent route. NOT FOR: anyone wanting a workspace, or an Irish buyer, since no Irish route is published.

A FAMILY HOUSING TWO PEOPLE, OR ONE PERSON WHO NEEDS A SPARE ROOM. A couple, a parent with a visiting grandchild, or an adult child with a home office of their own. This is a small house in the garden and should be planned as one, with a designer and a consent strategy from the outset rather than a delivery date. NOT FOR: a workspace buyer; a garden that could not physically take a two-bedroom footprint; or an Irish buyer, since the supplier serves South East England only.

A homeowner intending daily home-office use, prioritising the thickest available wall, prepared to commission insulation advice and a certified electrical connection separately, with a modest garden where a 16.64 m2 footprint leaves room to spare, and budgeting around EUR 13,610 for the delivered kit before groundworks and fit-out.

A HYBRID WORKER WHO WANTS AN OFFICE AND NOT A PROJECT. They are not choosing between materials or configurations — they want a room in the garden with a desk in it, from a supplier with a broad range and a straightforward product. THEIR PLANNING POSITION IS THE SIMPLEST IN THE RANGE, since office use raises no exemption question, leaving only the footprint to confirm. NOT FOR: two occupants or equipment, where the Large Garden Office Barcelona is the intended model; nor for a business with client visits, where the incidental-use condition becomes live.

An Irish homeowner in Kildare or a neighbouring county who works from home most days and wants one well-built room rather than the biggest room the garden will take. They care about thermal comfort and quiet — triple glazing is the reason they are looking at this supplier — and they want a single inclusive price with the electrics fitted and the walls painted rather than a shell and a list of trades to organise. They are comfortable that 12.5 m2 is a one-person space, and pleased that it leaves roughly 17.5 m2 of the combined allowance for a shed. They will ask two questions before signing: whether the concrete base is inside the price, and what covers the STRUCTURE as opposed to the roof membrane. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the Kildare-centred regional footprint; anyone comparing purely on cost per square metre, where this supplier is among the most expensive in the Atlas; anyone who needs a certified energy rating rather than a design claim.

An Irish homeowner in Kildare or a neighbouring county running a business or a full-time role from the garden, who needs room for a desk, storage, a printer and an occasional second person, and wants it warm and quiet enough to use every month of the year. They are paying a premium deliberately — for triple glazing, cedar cladding, SIP construction and an installed rather than a supplied price — and they value that the build is finished in five working days with the electrics fitted and the interior painted. They have checked that 12.4 m2 of the combined allowance remains for whatever else is in the garden. Before signing they will get the base position and the written guarantee document, and they will ask what covers the structure as distinct from the roof membrane. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone outside the regional footprint; anyone optimising cost per square metre; anyone who needs published U-values or a certified energy rating.

An Irish homeowner in Kildare or a neighbouring county with a clear back garden and a substantial requirement — a therapy or treatment practice, a studio, a family room, an office that hosts clients — who wants the largest building available without going into the planning process. They are paying a premium for triple glazing, SIP construction, cedar cladding and an installed price that carries the foundations, and they accept that at roughly EUR 1,600 per square metre this is not the value option. They have counted every existing structure on the plot against the 30 m2 combined allowance, and they will ask the supplier in writing whether the published 25 m2 is the EXTERNAL footprint, because on this model that single answer decides the planning route. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone whose garden already carries a shed or garage, since only 5 m2 of headroom remains; anyone outside the regional footprint; anyone comparing on price per square metre.

An Irish homeowner in Kildare or a neighbouring county with a completely clear back garden and a requirement that genuinely needs the extra metre — a large studio, a multi-room layout, a practice with a waiting area. Budget is not the constraint; specification and finish are what they are buying, and they want the building erected by the supplier's own team with the electrics fitted, the interior painted and the foundations inside the price. They are the buyer who most needs to do two things before signing: establish in writing whether the published 26.4 m2 is the EXTERNAL footprint, because the 3.6 m2 planning margin depends entirely on that answer, and ask what the EUR 6,100 step over the 25 m2 model actually buys, since no published specification difference explains it. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone with any existing structure in the garden; anyone outside the regional footprint; anyone for whom the 25 m2 model would do, which on the published evidence is most people considering this size.

SOMEONE WHO HAS SEEN A LUGARDE BUILDING AND WANTS THAT LOOK, AND IS WILLING TO DO THE LEGWORK. The range is bought on design and on the ability to specify a size, not on published information — so the buyer must be comfortable with a process that begins with finding the right dealer. THEY SHOULD EXPECT EVERY FIGURE TO COME FROM THAT DEALER. NOT FOR: a homeowner who needs to confirm exemption from published information; nor for anyone who wants a fixed price and a delivery date up front.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A MODEST GARDEN AND NO APPETITE FOR A PLANNING ARGUMENT. At roughly 7 m2 this building takes a corner rather than the garden, sits far inside the allowance, and is bought for pleasure rather than utility. THEY MAY ALSO HAVE AN EXISTING SHED they do not want to lose — which is precisely where a small footprint earns its place. NOT FOR: a home office, gym or studio, where the round plan and small area are the wrong shape twice over; nor for winter use without the separate insulation package.

A homeowner with a compact or already-occupied garden and a limited budget, wanting the largest plain room available for the money, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 6,290 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A CLEAR, SINGLE, INCIDENTAL USE IN MIND — a studio, a workshop, a music room, a garden office — and enough interest in design to look beyond the standard Irish catalogue. THEY ARE NOT TRYING TO SOLVE A HOUSING PROBLEM in the garden, which keeps the planning position simple. NOT FOR: a family looking to accommodate an adult child or a relative, where the Class 3A route and suppliers who address it directly are the honest answer.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A ROOM IN THE GARDEN AND HAS SOMEWHERE ELSE FOR THE TOOLS. Straightforward requirement, straightforward building — and the version of this model that leaves the most of the allowance for whatever is already standing. THEY ARE COMPARING THE TWO BARBADOS VERSIONS on price and on how much of the garden each uses, which is the right comparison to be making. NOT FOR: a household with nowhere to store garden equipment, where the storage version is the honest choice; nor for anyone who needs a published specification before making contact.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING THEIR FIRST AND ONLY GARDEN BUILDING. They know the room will have to absorb the garden tools as well unless storage is designed in, and they would rather pay for it once than watch the room fill up. THEY ARE PRACTICAL BUYERS comparing two versions of the same model, which is exactly the comparison the missing figures obstruct. NOT FOR: a garden that already has a shed, where the plain Barbados leaves more allowance intact; nor for a buyer who wants the largest possible room for the area, since the store takes part of it.

SOMEONE WHO HAS ALREADY FOUND A DEALER. In practice this range reaches Irish buyers through resellers, so the realistic buyer is one who has come across a Lugarde building through a UK or Irish garden-building retailer rather than through the manufacturer. THEY WILL BE RELYING ON THAT RETAILER FOR SIZE, PRICE, DELIVERY, ASSEMBLY AND WARRANTY — five things Atlas cannot supply. NOT FOR: a buyer starting from a blank page who wants to compare suppliers on published specifications; the range gives them nothing to compare with.

SOMEONE CHOOSING A MANUFACTURER FIRST AND A MODEL SECOND. That ordering suits this range, because the supplier-level position is well documented and the product-level position is not — a buyer who is satisfied with Lugarde as a company can then work through the designs with a dealer. THEY ARE BUYING A RELATIONSHIP AS MUCH AS A BUILDING. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing specific products across suppliers, where this range cannot be entered into the comparison at all.

SOMEONE ALREADY IN CONVERSATION WITH PINECA RATHER THAN SHOPPING FROM A LIST. Because nothing about this model's size can be established from published evidence, it is only usable to a buyer who has been quoted for it directly — at which point the insulated construction and the included insulation materials become real advantages. THEY SHOULD ASK FOR THE SAME THREE FIGURES the supplier publishes for its High-Quality specification. NOT FOR: a homeowner comparing options from a catalogue; nor for anyone who needs to check the exemption before making contact.

SOMEONE WILLING TO DO THEIR OWN RESEARCH RATHER THAN RELY ON A COMPARISON SITE. This range cannot be shopped from published data, so the buyer who does well here is one who visits a dealer, sees a building, asks for drawings and forms their own view. THEY TREAT THE ATLAS RECORD AS A STARTING POINT, not an answer. NOT FOR: a homeowner who needs certainty before engagement — there is none available for this model at present.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING A THREE-SEASON GARDEN BUILDING AND HAPPY FOR IT TO BE ONE. Spring to autumn use — a summer room, a hobby space, an occasional office — is what a solid log cabin does well as standard, and it avoids paying for an insulation package that will not be needed. THEY VALUE THE TIMBER AESTHETIC over thermal performance. NOT FOR: daily year-round working, without budgeting for all three insulation products; nor for a buyer who needs the internal dimension guaranteed before ordering.

A homeowner with a large garden, typically one with a pool, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting a 24 m2 room in the thickest available wall, willing to ask the supplier what the pool designation actually provides, and budgeting around EUR 13,780 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE BUYING A GARDEN FEATURE RATHER THAN A WORKSPACE. A 3 m round timber building is a place to sit at the end of the garden — a reading house, a sheltered seat, a summer room — and it is bought largely for how it looks from the house. THEY ARE NOT TRYING TO FIT A DESK, A FILING CABINET AND A SOFA IN, which is what makes the round plan acceptable. NOT FOR: a home office or gym, where the curved wall and small footprint work against them; nor for year-round use without the separate insulation package.

SOMEONE COMMISSIONING A BUILDING RATHER THAN BUYING ONE. The Prima system suits a household that has a size and a layout in mind and wants a Dutch log manufacturer to build to it — and who is comfortable dealing with an independent reseller rather than the manufacturer. THEY MUST BE PREPARED TO SPECIFY DOWN, since the published example is well over the exemption. THEY ALSO NEED TO BUDGET FOR INSULATION AS A SEPARATE LINE.
