NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a fixed, priced, exemption-ready product off a page; nor for anyone who needs a confirmed Irish delivery and installation route before ordering.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A ROOM AND NOTHING ELSE. No canopy, no attached shed — a straightforward garden room for work or hobbies, chosen partly because it keeps the decision and the paperwork simple. THEY MAY ALREADY HAVE A SHED they intend to keep, which is precisely why the plain layout suits them: it makes the fewest demands on the shared 30 m2. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants shelter at the door or storage attached, where the veranda and Super layouts exist; nor for anyone needing a published specification before enquiring.

A homeowner with a compact garden wanting a 12 m2 room with a sheltered doorway, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 7,750 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE CHOOSING BETWEEN LAYOUTS OF A ROOM THEY HAVE ALREADY SETTLED ON. They like the Jacob E and are deciding how much to add — which is a more advanced and more sensible stage of shopping than picking between suppliers, and the point at which the roofed-area arithmetic becomes the deciding factor. THEY WANT SHELTER AT THE DOOR without the cost of a shed. NOT FOR: a garden near its allowance, where any added roofed area is the wrong direction; nor for a buyer who needs storage as well, where the Super Jacob E layout is the intended answer.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT READS SPECIFICATIONS AND WILL NOTICE WHAT IS MISSING. Lugarde publishes one good thermal figure and no others, so the buyer who suits this supplier is one who will ask for the rest rather than assume the glazing figure represents the building. THEY ARE LIKELY TO END UP SPECIFYING THE FULL INSULATION PACKAGE. NOT FOR: a buyer who takes a published U-value as a statement about the whole envelope — here it is a statement about the windows only.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A WARM ROOM AND WANTS TO KNOW HOW BIG IT REALLY IS. The LAYLA line is the honest middle of the Pineca range — a proper insulated build at three sensible sizes with the internal floor published, which is the combination most buyers say they want and rarely get. THEY ARE PLANNING FURNITURE, so 10, 13 or 15 m2 of real floor is the number that matters to them. NOT FOR: intensive daily professional use, where the supplier points to SIPS or High-Quality insulation; nor for a buyer who needs a U-value.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A GARDEN ROOM AND HAS NOT OVER-THOUGHT IT. No configuration, no material preference, no games table to accommodate — a room, in the garden, for whatever the household needs it for. THAT IS THE MAJORITY BUYER, and the plain models are what they should be looking at. THEY WILL DECIDE ON PRICE AND PHOTOGRAPHS, so the one thing worth insisting on is the footprint. NOT FOR: a specific brief — office, poolhouse, workshop, storage — where the configured records in the same range are the intended answer.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden who wants the largest possible enclosed room plus integrated storage without giving ground to a veranda, is prepared to ask the supplier for the internal split before ordering, and is budgeting around EUR 10,420 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE FURNISHING A GARDEN, NOT SOLVING A SPACE PROBLEM. The buyer who does well with this range treats the building as part of the landscaping — chosen for how it sits and how it looks — and is prepared to specify the technical side afterwards. THEY WILL USUALLY WANT THE INSULATED BUILD if the room is for daily use, and should budget accordingly. NOT FOR: a buyer whose first question is cost per square metre, which this range cannot answer from published information.

SOMEONE WHO TRUSTS A SUPPLIER RELATIONSHIP MORE THAN A SPECIFICATION SHEET. That is a reasonable way to buy from a manufacturer with a long history and a distinctive range — but it does place weight on choosing the right dealer, since the dealer is effectively the only source of information. THEY SHOULD KEEP EVERYTHING IN WRITING. NOT FOR: a buyer who expects to verify claims independently before committing, which this supplier's documentation does not currently allow.

A CAREFUL BUYER WHO ASKS THE SECOND QUESTION. The first question — how big is it — has no published answer here; the second — on what basis is that measured — is the one that actually protects them, and it applies to every quotation they receive from this supplier. THEY WILL PROBABLY ASK FOR A DIMENSIONED DRAWING. NOT FOR: a buyer who takes a stated area at face value, which in this range would be unsafe across two different wall systems.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN AND A REAL PROGRAMME FOR THE BUILDING. Thirty square metres is a studio, a two-person office or a room and a store, and at this size the exemption survives only on a clear plot — which is a genuine and checkable condition rather than a vague one. THEY WILL WANT THE INSULATED SPECIFICATION and should say so at order. NOT FOR: an ordinary suburban garden with a shed in it, where this building cannot be exempt; nor for a buyer who has not decided between a summer shell and a winter room.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A FLEXIBLE BUDGET AND A FIRM VIEW ON WHAT THEY WANT. Bespoke suits people who would rather adjust the specification than the design, and who are not working to a fixed ceiling that a quotation might overshoot. THEY WILL WANT SEVERAL QUOTATIONS AT THE SAME STATED SIZE. NOT FOR: a first-time buyer trying to work out what a garden room costs — this range will not tell them, and an Irish supplier with published prices will.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH AN AVERAGE SUBURBAN GARDEN AND ONE ROOM'S WORTH OF NEED. At 15 m2 the building fits without dominating, the exemption is not marginal, and the cost of the separate insulation package is proportionate to a smaller structure. THEY LIKE THE LOG AESTHETIC — which is what Lugarde actually sells — rather than a contemporary clad pod. NOT FOR: a buyer wanting a large multi-use room, where the Zurich or a bespoke Prima build is the route; nor for anyone needing a confirmed installed price in Ireland before committing.

A PRACTICAL HOUSEHOLD WITH A BUILDER THEY TRUST, or the skills to do it themselves. Buying the building and arranging the base and assembly locally can work out well, and it puts control of quality in the owner's hands. THEY NEED TO BE REALISTIC ABOUT THE WEIGHT AND SCALE of a solid log kit. NOT FOR: a homeowner expecting a turnkey installation, which this manufacturer does not offer and cannot guarantee through any dealer.

SOMEONE WHO WILL WALK OUT TO THIS BUILDING IN THE RAIN MOST DAYS. That is the practical case for a covered front on a working garden room, and it is a requirement people usually discover after their first winter rather than before it. THEY WANT A DAILY-USE ROOM WITH A SENSIBLE ENTRANCE, not a summer house. NOT FOR: a garden close to its allowance, where an unmeasured canopy is exactly the wrong kind of unknown; nor for a buyer who will accept a room-only figure as the whole answer.

SOMEONE COMFORTABLE BUYING FROM A UK RETAILER. Plenty of Irish households do it routinely and are unfazed by arranging carriage — for them the reseller model is an inconvenience rather than an obstacle, and it opens up a range the Irish market does not carry. THEY SHOULD PRICE DELIVERY AS A LINE ITEM, not an afterthought, on a heavy timber kit. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a single Irish contact responsible for supply, delivery, assembly and warranty — that structure does not exist here.

NOBODY SHOULD BE ORDERING FROM THIS RECORD AS IT STANDS. A homeowner who wants an OAK should work from the 44 mm record for a summer room or the Insulated record for a winter one — both name their construction, and at this supplier the construction cannot be changed later. THE RECORD'S VALUE IS AS A WARNING that a supplier can publish two areas for one product on the same page. NOT FOR: any buyer at the point of order, until the area conflict and the wall specification are both resolved in writing.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS AN OFFICE AND HAS FOUND A MODEL FAMILY THAT LETS THEM CHOOSE HOW MUCH ELSE TO ADD. They may start here and move to the veranda or shed-and-porch layout, or the reverse — which is a sensible way to shop, provided the footprints of each are obtained. THEY WILL BE WORKING IN IT DAILY, so the thermal question matters to them more than the area does. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the specification settled before contact; nor for a business with visiting clients, where the incidental-use condition becomes live.

SOMEONE WHO LIKES LOOKING AFTER THINGS. A solid timber garden building suits a household that is comfortable with a maintenance routine and prefers a material that ages rather than degrades — the same instinct that chooses timber windows over uPVC. THEY WILL PROBABLY KEEP THE BUILDING FOR TWENTY YEARS. NOT FOR: a homeowner who wants a maintenance-free product, where composite-clad insulated rooms are the honest alternative.

REALISTICALLY, NOBODY IS SHOPPING FOR THIS RECORD BY NAME — a product code is not something a homeowner searches for, and the equivalent building is almost certainly available under one of the range's named models. THE RECORD IS MORE USEFUL AS A WARNING THAN AS AN OPTION: it shows what a catalogue capture looks like when it crosses markets. NOT FOR: any buyer at present, until the record is reconciled against the English range and an Irish route is established.

SOMEONE PATIENT. This is a purchase that will take several exchanges before a price exists, and the buyer who is happy with that is usually one who cares about the building itself rather than about getting it done by spring. THEY OFTEN COME TO LUGARDE HAVING SEEN ONE, not having searched for one. NOT FOR: a homeowner replacing a rotten shed in a hurry, where an Irish supplier with stock sizes and a delivery date is the better fit.

A HOUSEHOLD IN AN ESTABLISHED SUBURB WITH A GARDEN THAT IS PLEASANT BUT NOT LARGE. For them the question is not how big a building they can have but how much garden they are willing to give up — and a supplier who builds to a specified size lets them answer it precisely. THEY WILL WANT TO SEE THE FOOTPRINT PEGGED OUT before ordering. NOT FOR: a homeowner who wants the whole thing settled from a website; nor for a plot where the open-space test is already marginal.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH AN AWKWARD GARDEN. Where a standard 4 × 3 m box will not fit — a narrow strip, a corner, a boundary to respect, an existing shed to work around — a supplier that builds to a specified size is worth the extra process. THEY ARE COMFORTABLE BUYING THROUGH A DEALER and treating the model name as a starting design rather than a product. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to compare published sizes and prices across suppliers before making contact, which this range does not support.

SOMEONE CHOOSING ON DESIGN FIRST AND WORKING BACKWARDS TO THE SPECIFICATION. That is a legitimate way to buy a garden building — it is a visible object in a garden for twenty years — and Lugarde's range rewards it. THE BUYER MUST THEN ACCEPT A LONGER PROCESS: the design is chosen from the catalogue, everything else comes from a dealer. NOT FOR: a homeowner working to a fixed budget and a deadline, where an Irish supplier with published prices and lead times removes most of the uncertainty.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT ALREADY HAS A SHED AND DOES NOT WANT TO LOSE IT. That is a common and under-served position: the combined allowance means the existing structure eats into the budget of square metres, and most catalogues start at a size that leaves no room. A SUPPLIER WHO BUILDS TO A NUMBER SOLVES IT. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs to compare several quotations quickly, where variable sizing makes the comparison unreliable.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A PROPER ROOM RATHER THAN A POD, AND HAS THE GARDEN FOR IT. Twenty square metres is a working office plus a sitting area, or a gym, or a music room — and at that size the exemption is still comfortably in reach if the plot is otherwise clear. THEY ARE PREPARED TO WORK THROUGH A DEALER AND TO BUY INSULATION SEPARATELY. NOT FOR: a homeowner whose garden already holds a large shed, where 20 m2 leaves little headroom; nor for anyone who needs a fixed, non-configurable size for certainty.

A HOUSEHOLD SOLVING THE WHOLE GARDEN IN ONE PURCHASE. They need a room and they need somewhere for the mower, the bikes and the garden tools — and they would rather have one building than two mismatched ones. THAT IS A SENSIBLE INSTINCT, and combining does not cost them anything against the allowance that two separate structures would not. WHAT IT DOES IS CONCENTRATE THE UNKNOWN into a single unmeasured total. NOT FOR: a garden already close to 30 m2, where a three-element building is the least likely to fit; nor for a buyer who already has a shed worth keeping.

A SNOOKER PLAYER WITH A LARGE GARDEN AND NOWHERE INDOORS TO PUT A TABLE. That is a specific and unusual brief, and it is the only reason to consider a building of this kind — the room exists to hold one object properly. THEY WILL HAVE ALREADY MEASURED THE TABLE AND THE CUE CLEARANCE, which makes them well placed to ask the supplier the right question about the external footprint. NOT FOR: a garden with any existing structure, where the combined allowance is likely to fail; nor for a household that wants the room to serve other uses, since the plan is dictated by the table.

SOMEONE WHO OUTGREW THE IDEA OF A SHED BUT NOT THE BUDGET FOR ONE. A hobbyist, a home worker with a laptop and some storage, or a student needing quiet — a single occupant with a defined task and a modest garden. They are stepping up one size from the smallest model because they want a wall for shelving or a printer, not because they need a second zone. THEY ARE COMFORTABLE WITH A SIMPLE PRODUCT: no configurator, no design consultation, a published size and an established shed-and-garden supplier. NOT FOR: two people working simultaneously, gym or studio use, or a buyer who needs documented insulation performance for winter occupancy.

A SINGLE OCCUPANT WITH TWO ACTIVITIES THAT CAN SIT SIDE BY SIDE. A home worker who also paints, sews, models or repairs — desk at one end, bench at the other, everything along one wall. They want the largest room in a simple range rather than the smallest room in a complicated one, and they are content with a straightforward shed-and-garden supplier rather than a design-led manufacturer. THEY ALSO WANT THE PLANNING QUESTION TO STAY CLOSED: at 8.92 m2 it does, whatever else is in the garden. NOT FOR: two simultaneous users, gym or studio use that needs clear floor, or a buyer who requires documented insulation performance before committing to winter occupancy.

A CAUTIOUS FIRST BUYER WITH A SMALL GARDEN AND A SINGLE PURPOSE. Someone who wants to get out of the spare bedroom for two or three days a week, who does not want a planning conversation, and who would rather spend less and keep most of the garden. They are choosing the smallest thing that will work, deliberately. THEY VALUE CERTAINTY OVER SPECIFICATION: knowing the building is comfortably exempt matters more to them than knowing its U-value — which is fortunate, because Atlas holds no U-value. NOT FOR: anyone who needs two functions in the room, anyone tall enough to feel a 2.44 m depth, or a buyer who wants documented thermal performance for winter use.

A homeowner with a large open garden able to accommodate a 33 m2 structure, prepared to seek planning permission or clarify the veranda question locally, wanting substantial covered outdoor space alongside a 19 m2 room, and budgeting around EUR 13,440 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a broadly square area of garden or an awkward corner to use, few existing outbuildings, wanting 19 m2 in the thickest available wall at the lowest published price for that combination, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 11,200 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS SOMEWHERE TO SIT OUT IN APRIL AND OCTOBER. The veranda is the reason they are looking at this model rather than a plain room — shelter without being indoors, which is the whole appeal of a summer house in an Irish garden. THEY ARE BUYING FOR LEISURE, and are the buyer least likely to have thought about the allowance at all. NOT FOR: year-round working use, where nothing thermal is published; nor for guest sleeping, which is a different consent route; nor for a garden already close to 30 m2.

A homeowner with a medium garden and few existing outbuildings, who will use the covered porch as much as the room, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 7,750 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a clear garden and no existing outbuildings, wanting the largest room available without planning permission, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 14,810 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a shallow garden or a boundary run of about 6 m, wanting a small room with a roofed outdoor area attached, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 5,600 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a shallow garden or a boundary run of about 6 m, wanting a small room with sheltered seating attached for seasonal use, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 6,200 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a garden large enough to give up 25.52 m2 and few or no existing outbuildings, who is comfortable arranging a base and assembly themselves, who wants sheltered outdoor seating more than a working room, and whose intended use is seasonal rather than year-round. Budget around EUR 7,460 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a clear garden and no existing outbuildings, willing to give effectively the whole statutory allowance to one structure, wanting a 15 m2 studio for seasonal use, comfortable arranging base and assembly across a 577 x 502 cm envelope, and budgeting around EUR 8,610 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A FAMILY WHOSE TABLE HAS BEEN FOLDED AGAINST A GARAGE WALL FOR YEARS. Table tennis is the classic household game that never quite has anywhere to live, and a building sized for it is the direct answer — usually bought for children and teenagers, and used by everyone. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN and are not otherwise short of storage, which is what makes the footprint affordable against the allowance. NOT FOR: a small garden or one with an existing shed, where a long-plan games room is the least likely product to fit; nor for a buyer who needs the room to double as an office.

A homeowner with a modest garden or an existing shed to work around, wanting a plain enclosed room of about 12 m2 for storage, a hobby or seasonal work, comfortable arranging base and assembly, budgeting around EUR 6,980 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A PRACTICAL BUYER WHO WANTS THE FUNCTION AND NOT THE BADGE. Shelter over the patio, at the lowest price the range offers, from a recognised brand — and a willingness to accept a base specification because nothing published justifies paying more. THEY ARE WELL SERVED BY THIS RECORD'S HONESTY: the editions cannot be told apart on evidence, so the cheapest is a defensible default. NOT FOR: a household that needs an enclosed room; nor for one whose garden allowance is already committed, where a cover of ordinary size may not fit within what remains.

SOMEONE UPGRADING AN OUTDOOR LIVING SPACE RATHER THAN SOLVING A SHORTAGE OF ROOMS. They already use the terrace, they want control over sun and rain, and they are prepared to pay for a mechanism rather than a plain roof — a discretionary, quality-led purchase. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO ASSUME AN ADJUSTABLE STRUCTURE FALLS OUTSIDE THE RULES, which is the assumption most worth challenging. NOT FOR: a household needing enclosed, heatable space; nor for a garden where the allowance is nearly used, since the prudent reading counts the whole covered area.

A BUYER COMPARING TWO NEARLY IDENTICAL QUOTATIONS AND TRYING TO WORK OUT WHAT THEY ARE PAYING FOR. That is the situation this record exists to describe honestly: the catalogue cannot distinguish the editions, so the comparison has to be made from supplier documentation rather than from published specifications. THEY WANT AN ADJUSTABLE ROOF OVER AN EXISTING TERRACE and are willing to pay for engineering — a discretionary purchase for an outdoor space they already use. NOT FOR: anyone needing an enclosed room; nor for a buyer who expects the model name to tell them what they are getting.

A BUYER AT THE TOP OF A COVER RANGE, SPENDING ACCORDINGLY. They want the best version of an adjustable-roof terrace and have the budget to take the flagship without much scrutiny — which makes them precisely the buyer who should ask what the flagship actually provides, since the catalogue cannot say. THEIR TERRACE IS LIKELY LARGE, which also makes the unpublished covered footprint the most consequential omission for them, since a big cover eats a big share of the 30 m2. NOT FOR: a homeowner needing an enclosed room, or one whose allowance is nearly committed.

SOMEONE COVERING A TERRACE THAT SITS TIGHT AGAINST THE HOUSE OR A BOUNDARY. The flat profile is chosen for how it sits rather than for what it does differently — a contemporary house, a narrow side terrace, or a neighbour whose light matters. THEY START WITH ONE ADVANTAGE OVER EVERY OTHER BUYER IN THIS RANGE: they know which height limit applies to them. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the extra headroom a pitched form could allow, since the flat roof commits them to the tighter 3 m test; nor for anyone needing an enclosed room.

A DESIGN-CONSCIOUS BUYER WILLING TO MANAGE A CONTINENTAL PURCHASE. They like the German brand and the contemporary look, and they are prepared to run their own siting and compliance process because the supplier publishes no Irish route — which in practice means either an experienced self-builder or someone working with an architect. NOT FOR: a homeowner who wants a delivered, installed, locally supported product with a stated size; nor for anyone who needs to demonstrate exemption compliance before ordering, since nothing measurable is published.

SOMEONE WITH A PATIO THEY ALREADY USE AND WEATHER THEY CANNOT RELY ON. The requirement is shelter over an existing outdoor space — dining, seating, a barbecue area — rather than a room, and a cover is the correct and cheaper answer to it. THE RISK IS THAT THEY NEVER THINK OF THIS AS A PLANNING DECISION, which is exactly why the allowance question belongs in front of them. NOT FOR: a workspace, a gym or any use needing enclosure, heating or security — an open-sided cover provides none of those; nor for a household planning a garden room later, unless the combined total is checked first.

A BUYER TRADING UP WITHIN A COVER RANGE RATHER THAN CHOOSING BETWEEN CATEGORIES. They have already decided they want a terrace cover and are now selecting an edition — which makes them exactly the buyer who needs to know that the catalogue provides no basis for that selection. THEY SHOULD ARRIVE AT THE SUPPLIER WITH A LIST OF SPECIFICATION QUESTIONS rather than a model preference. NOT FOR: a homeowner who has not yet worked out whether they need a cover or a room — that decision comes first and carries the real consequences.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT ENTERTAINS OUTSIDE AND HAS GIVEN UP ON THE WEATHER. They already have the terrace, the furniture and the habit; what they lack is shelter, and a cover is the direct answer. THE CRITICAL THING FOR THEM IS SEQUENCE: if a garden office or gym is also on the horizon, the cover should be sized with that in mind, because both draw on the same 30 m2. NOT FOR: anyone needing an enclosed, heatable, securable space — that is a garden room, and this supplier's Helios or the ModPod pods are the relevant records.

SOMEONE HOUSING A RELATIVE AND SHOPPING IN THE WRONG AISLE. They have found a cabin that looks like a house at a garden-building price, and the appeal is real — but the regulatory route is the dwelling route, with the cost, timeline and minimum-size threshold that implies. THE MOST USEFUL THING THIS RECORD CAN DO FOR THEM is redirect the search before a deposit is paid. NOT FOR: anyone expecting to install it as exempt development. FOR A GENUINE DAY ROOM, a smaller exempt garden room from a supplier publishing its footprint is both cheaper and simpler.

A golfer with a long garden of at least 9 m clear run, prepared to seek planning permission, who will specify and buy simulator hardware separately, will confirm internal height with the supplier, and is budgeting around EUR 17,160 for the delivered shell alone.

A golfer with a large garden, prepared to seek planning permission, who will specify and buy simulator hardware separately, will confirm internal height with the supplier, and is budgeting around EUR 16,360 for the delivered shell alone.

A UK HOMEOWNER WITH A SMALL GARDEN WHO WANTS THE PROJECT HANDLED. Someone who would rather pay an established manufacturer to deliver and install a finished room than manage a base, a kit and a joiner. They want a quiet place to work, they have limited outdoor space, and the smallest model in a well-known range is a low-risk way in. THEY ARE BUYING REPUTATION AND PROCESS, not published performance data — which is the honest description of this record, since no U-values exist for it. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on current evidence, because the delivery radius does not reach Ireland; nor for anyone needing two functions in the room, since under 7.56 m2 gross leaves very little once the walls are built.

A UK HOME WORKER BUYING THEIR FIRST PROPER OFFICE AND WANTING SOMEONE ELSE TO BUILD IT. They want a room they can furnish normally rather than a booth, they have a garden that can take a 3.3 m square building without dominating it, and they would rather buy from a large manufacturer with an installed price than manage trades themselves. THEY ARE NOT TECHNICAL BUYERS: they will not ask for a U-value, which is fortunate because none is published — but they should ask, because winter usability is the one thing this record cannot evidence. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner on current evidence, given the delivery radius; nor for a buyer who needs the room to serve two functions.

A homeowner with a budget above GBP 30k who wants a large, properly finished room from a well-known manufacturer, and who values a long trading record and an installed service over reading specification sheets. Suits a permanent home office or garden gym in regular year-round use.

A UK homeowner with a compact urban or suburban garden who needs one quiet, warm room for daily use — typically a home office or hobby room — and wants it finished and working rather than delivered as a kit. Budget around GBP 9,000 all-in. Values a single-day installation and a supplier who includes the foundation and electrics rather than quoting them separately.

A UK homeowner working from home most days who needs a real office rather than a desk in a corner, and who is price-sensitive enough to choose Sanctum's entry range over its composite-clad Urban line. Comfortable with a painted or clad timber finish that will need occasional maintenance, in exchange for saving several thousand pounds against the maintenance-free composite options.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS TO SEE THE BUILDING BEFORE BUYING IT. That is the deciding advantage here — three showrooms across three provinces, one walk-in — and it suits a household spending five figures who is not comfortable ordering from photographs. A SQUARE PLAN IN FOUR SIZES covers most single-room briefs. THEY SHOULD USE THE SHOWROOM VISIT TO RESOLVE THE WALL SPECIFICATION, which is the one thing the catalogue leaves contradictory. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs a confirmed year-round specification from published information; nor for anyone who takes the supplier's own planning wording at face value.

SOMEONE WHOSE LIVELIHOOD DEPENDS ON THE ROOM BEING USABLE EVERY DAY OF THE YEAR. Pineca recommends this specification for a PERMANENT WORKSPACE or residential use, and the published U-values let a buyer verify that claim rather than take it on trust — which is the whole reason to choose it over cheaper insulated options. THEY WILL BE COMPARING QUOTATIONS TECHNICALLY, and this is the record that gives them the numbers to do it with. NOT FOR: an occasional summer studio, where the money is better spent elsewhere in the Pineca ladder; nor for a buyer who needs the usable internal floor confirmed before committing.

A REMOTE OR HYBRID WORKER IN IRELAND WHO NEEDS THE ROOM TO DO MORE THAN ONE JOB. Someone whose home office also has to serve as a gym, a music room or a quiet space for study, and who wants a building sized for that rather than a 3 m x 3 m box. They are practical rather than technical: they want a straightforward Irish supplier, a sensible size and no planning application, and they are content to ask the specification questions themselves rather than needing the whole build published in advance. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants documented U-values and a published warranty before committing — none of that is held here — or anyone whose garden is already crowded enough that 18 m2 plus existing structures would approach the 30 m2 combined limit.

A DESIGN-LED BUYER FURNISHING A GARDEN, NOT SOLVING A SPACE SHORTAGE. Someone who has seen the form, wants exactly that, and is willing to run a cross-border enquiry to get it. They are not price-per-square-metre buyers — a curved shell costs more to build and delivers less usable floor than a rectangle of the same footprint, and they know it. THEY WILL NEED TO BE PERSISTENT ON NUMBERS: with no published dimensions, height or price, everything that matters has to be extracted in correspondence, and they will also be arranging Irish delivery, base and installation themselves. NOT FOR: a buyer maximising desk space, comparing on cost per m2, or needing certainty about exempted development before committing.

A COMMISSIONING BUYER RATHER THAN A SHOPPING ONE. Someone who has decided on the iglu form and is prepared to engage Iglucraft in a made-to-order conversation about size, layout and siting — and who understands that the planning position will be decided inside that conversation, not looked up beforehand. They should come to it having already measured every existing structure in their back garden, so they can state their remaining allowance as a hard constraint on the design. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to compare two Iglucraft models against each other, since Atlas records no difference between them; or anyone who needs a fixed price and a specification sheet before starting.

SOMEONE MAXIMISING A CLEAR PLOT. A homeowner with a genuinely empty back garden, a specific need for a large room, and the discipline to check the footprint before committing rather than after. They are optimising for space above all else and are prepared to accept that the resulting building consumes their entire garden-structure allowance in one go — no future shed, no future studio, nothing else without permission. NOT FOR: a garden that already holds a shed or garage; a buyer who wants comparison data on insulation, warranty or price, none of which is published; or, on current evidence, an Irish buyer at all, since no Irish purchasing route is held.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE. THE ONE THING THAT CAN BE SAID: a buyer who pursues a design-led cabin with no published technical data is choosing on appearance first and will have to do the specification work themselves, in correspondence, before they can compare it with anything. That suits someone for whom the look of the building is the primary requirement and who has the patience to extract numbers from a supplier — and it does not suit anyone trying to weigh cost per square metre, thermal performance or planning position across a shortlist, because this record can contribute nothing to that exercise.

A BUYER WHO HAS FOUND THE RIGHT SIZE AND STILL HAS ONE QUESTION LEFT. The 4 × 5 m LILLE is a well-judged garden room on plan and on planning; the only outstanding matter is which construction they are being quoted, and that is a single email to the supplier. THEY SHOULD ASK FOR THE SKU AND THE WALL CLASS TOGETHER. NOT FOR: anyone comparing prices across suppliers from this record, since the figure could belong to either the insulated or the uninsulated build.

SOMEONE WHO WILL WORK IN IT THROUGH AN IRISH WINTER. That is the deciding requirement, and it is the one this record meets where most of the range does not — a household replacing a spare bedroom with a proper detached office, five days a week, all year. THEY HAVE USUALLY ALREADY LEARNED that a log cabin and an insulated room are different products. NOT FOR: an occasional summer studio, where the uninsulated classes cost materially less; nor for a buyer who needs a published U-value to compare against a SIPS or frame-built room.

A HYBRID WORKER WHO WANTS THE DECISION TO BE SIMPLE. One desk, a small garden, no appetite for a planning conversation — and a preference for buying from somewhere they can drive to. The Irish showroom network is a large part of the appeal: they can see the build quality rather than infer it from photographs. THEY SHOULD STILL ASK FOR THE HEIGHT, which is the only exemption condition this product leaves open. NOT FOR: two occupants, a gym, or anyone who will outgrow 9 m2 within a year — the Longford at 23.60 m2 is the honest next step.

A homeowner with a large garden corner able to accommodate a 50 m2 structure, prepared to seek planning permission, and willing to question the supplier closely about what the published envelope contains and why it publishes the same room area as the half-depth version, budgeting around EUR 14,730 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING A GARDEN BUILDING FOR SUMMER LIVING RATHER THAN FOR WORK. Somewhere to sit, eat and entertain, positioned to catch the sun in a corner of a large garden — a leisure purchase, and one where the specification is judged by eye rather than by U-value. THEY ARE THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO OVERLOOK THE ALLOWANCE ENTIRELY, because a summer house feels less like a building than an office does. NOT FOR: a small garden, where a large corner plan is the least efficient use of the limit; nor for year-round working use, since nothing thermal is published.

A homeowner wanting a two-level garden building on a compact footprint — typically for occasional guest use or a studio with storage above — who understands that overnight accommodation falls outside the exemption and is prepared to seek planning permission, and who is budgeting around EUR 16,620 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

TWO PEOPLE WORKING FROM HOME FULL TIME. Two desks, two screens, storage and somewhere to take a call without being overheard — the requirement that pushes a household from a study to a building. THEY WILL USE IT DAILY THROUGH THE WINTER, which makes the unpublished thermal specification the gap that matters most to them, more than the area does. NOT FOR: occasional use, where a smaller office model is proportionate; nor for a garden with an existing garage, where a large footprint and the combined allowance collide.

A homeowner intending daily home-office use in a garden where ground is at a premium, prioritising enclosed area and the thickest available wall over covered outdoor space, prepared to commission insulation advice and a certified electrical connection separately, and budgeting around EUR 8,180 for the delivered kit before groundworks and fit-out.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT HAS DECIDED IT NEEDS A BIG ROOM AND IS NOW CHOOSING BETWEEN NEAR-IDENTICAL OPTIONS. That is the honest description of this record's buyer: four large models, four letters, and no published basis for the choice. THEY HAVE THE GARDEN FOR IT and are shopping on price and appearance. THE ONE THING WORTH DOING DIFFERENTLY is asking for the footprints together rather than one at a time. NOT FOR: a garden with existing structures; nor for a buyer who wants to compare before making contact, since the comparison cannot be made from published information.

SOMEONE AT THE END OF A SHORTLIST RATHER THAN THE START OF ONE. They know they want a large room from this supplier and are working through the letters — which is the point at which the missing dimensions stop being an abstraction and start costing time. THEY HAVE A LARGE, PREFERABLY EMPTY GARDEN and a multi-use requirement. NOT FOR: a plot with a garage or substantial shed, where the combined allowance is the binding constraint; nor for anyone who needs certainty before enquiring.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING ONE BUILDING TO SOLVE SEVERAL PROBLEMS. Two people working from home, or a workspace that becomes a gym or family room outside office hours — the requirement that justifies the upper end of a range rather than the middle. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN, and are the buyer for whom the combined-allowance question is most live, since a large room plus an existing shed is exactly the combination that breaches 30 m2. NOT FOR: a small or already-built garden; nor for a buyer unwilling to obtain the footprint before ordering.

SOMEONE COMPARING TWO SIMILAR QUOTATIONS AND TRYING TO SEE THE DIFFERENCE. That is the practical situation this record describes: the Hansa E and F look alike in the catalogue, and the choice will be made from supplier drawings rather than from published specifications. THEY WANT A LARGE, WELL-BUILT ROOM and have the garden for it. NOT FOR: a plot with existing structures, where either large model risks the combined allowance; nor for a buyer who will accept a letter designation without a dimensioned plan behind it.

A homeowner with a large garden, prepared to seek planning permission, needing a single very large room for games, studio or workshop use, prepared to commission heating and insulation advice separately, and budgeting around EUR 18,520 for the delivered kit before substantial groundworks.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting the largest possible enclosed room along a boundary without giving ground to a veranda, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 16,020 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A MODERN HOUSE AND A REQUIREMENT FOR REAL SPACE. Two working adults, or a room that serves as office, gym and family space in turn — and a preference for clean contemporary lines rather than a chalet look. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN and are buying at the top of a broad range. THE QUESTION THEY SHOULD ASK FIRST IS THE ROOF, since a flat or mono-pitch form caps them at 3 m and nothing published says which this is. NOT FOR: a small garden; nor for a period house where the traditional forms in the same range sit better.

NOBODY SHOULD BE SHORTLISTING FROM THIS RECORD. A buyer interested in Gardenhouse24 should work from the six models that carry a verified internal floor area — Carin 44 A at 8.35 m2, Monaco 28 at 8.55, Mayo Office Box M at 8.2, CARLOW 44 A at 19.11, DUBLIN 70 at 22.15 and RAMSAY 70 A ALU at 22.62. THE RECORD'S VALUE IS AS A FLAG that a catalogue entry can name a product the supplier no longer lists. NOT FOR: any buyer, until the supplier listing is confirmed.

A HOUSEHOLD PUTTING A GYM IN THE GARDEN, OR AN OFFICE THAT WILL ALSO TAKE EQUIPMENT. Twenty-five square metres is a genuine training space, and a gym is a use where three-season performance is often acceptable — people heat up when they use it, and nobody sits still for eight hours. THEY WILL WANT THE LARGEST VARIANT, and should know it uses almost the whole allowance. NOT FOR: a daily desk-based office through an Irish winter, where the walls would need to be addressed; nor for a garden that already carries a shed and wants the 5 × 5.

SOMEONE BUYING A GARDEN ROOM AS A PLACE TO BE OUTSIDE, NOT ONLY INSIDE. A family who will use the covered area as much as the room — summer evenings, sheltered seating, a spot the children can use in the rain. That is a sound reason to choose this over a plain cabin, and it is why the product exists. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO MISCALCULATE THEIR ALLOWANCE, because the feature they are paying for is the part they will not think to measure. NOT FOR: a garden already close to the combined 30 m2, where the patio is the difference between exempt and not.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT NEEDS ONE BUILDING TO DO SEVERAL JOBS AND HAS AN OTHERWISE EMPTY GARDEN. Office and gym, or workspace and family room — the uses that need 4 m of depth. They want a timber cabin rather than a clad frame, and they value being able to see it in a showroom first. THEY MUST BE WILLING TO ASK ONE UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTION at that showroom: is 5.9 m × 4 m the inside or the outside? NOT FOR: a garden with an existing shed or garage of any size, where the 6.40 m2 headroom disappears; nor for a buyer who wants certainty without asking for a dimensioned plan.

Someone who wants a compact, genuinely self-contained unit — a garden annexe, a studio flat for an adult child, a short-let — and who values arriving-complete over specifying every detail themselves. They are attracted by heating, lighting, a kitchen and a bathroom all included at one price, and they are realistic that a building with those things in it is a small dwelling rather than a garden office, whatever its footprint. They will obtain a dimensioned drawing rather than trusting the numeral, and they will take advice on whether the use test can be met before relying on any exemption. A Republic of Ireland buyer will confirm cross-border delivery, installation and VAT treatment in writing before committing. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who wants a plain heated garden office and would be paying for a kitchen and bathroom they will never use; anyone who needs the exemption to hold, since the use condition is the likely obstacle; anyone who needs a U-value.

Someone adding a compact independent unit — a studio annexe for a family member, a home-and-work combination, or a small let — who wants the building complete on arrival rather than a shell to fit out. They are drawn to a single price covering heating, lighting, kitchen, bathroom and installation, and they have the budget to treat foundations and service connections as a separate line. They understand that this model sits on the boundary of the exemption on the supplier's own scale statement, and that the honest position is unresolved until a dimensioned drawing exists — so they will ask for one before anything else, and they will take advice on the use condition given the kitchen and bathroom. A Republic of Ireland buyer will confirm cross-border delivery, installation and VAT in writing first. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone needing certainty on exempted development before ordering; anyone wanting a plain garden office; anyone who needs a U-value.

Someone adding a small independent annexe — an adult child staying at home, an elderly parent moving closer, or a short-let unit — who wants it to arrive heated and fitted rather than as a shell they must finish. They are budgeting separately for groundworks and service connections, and they understand that a kitchen and a bathroom make the use non-incidental, so they are prepared for a planning conversation rather than assuming an exemption. Crucially, they will ask for the external footprint in writing before anything else, because on this model the difference between under and over the 30 m2 threshold cannot be read off the name. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone who wants a garden office and would be paying for a kitchen and bathroom they will not use; anyone in the Republic needing delivery confirmed now; anyone comparing on cost per square metre, which cannot be calculated without an area.

Someone adding a genuine second living space on their own site — accommodation for a family member, a long-term let, or a home-and-studio combination — who wants the building to arrive heated, wired, plumbed and fitted rather than as a shell. They have already accepted that this is a planning application rather than an exemption, on both the area and the use grounds, and they are budgeting foundations, drainage, water and power separately from the building price. They will obtain a dimensioned drawing before signing, because the model numeral is not a measurement, and a Republic of Ireland buyer will confirm cross-border delivery, installation and VAT treatment in writing first. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone wanting an exempted garden room — this model fails that test twice over; anyone wanting a plain office and paying for a kitchen and bathroom they will not use; anyone who needs published thermal performance before committing.

Someone creating a one or two bedroom independent unit on their own site — family accommodation, a long-stay guest annexe, or a let — who wants it to arrive heated, wired, plumbed and fitted rather than as a shell. They are attracted by the single price and the short installation, and they are budgeting separately for foundations, drainage, water and power. Critically, they are the buyer most likely to have READ THE SUPPLIER'S PLANNING CLAIM and taken it at face value, so they are the buyer who most needs to test it: a kitchen and a bathroom make the use non-incidental, which takes the building outside the 30 m2 exemption regardless of area, and the 32-45 m2 auxiliary-dwelling route is a different application with its own conditions and an end date. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone wanting a garden office; anyone who cannot get a definitive answer on which collection and which model they are buying; a Republic of Ireland buyer who needs delivery confirmed before committing.

NO TYPICAL HOMEOWNER CAN BE DESCRIBED FOR THIS RECORD, and describing one would be an invention the evidence does not support. The certified AM-001 layer records the product as UNMATCHED to any published model, so there is no confirmed size, no confirmed layout and no confirmed price to match a buyer against. WHAT CAN BE SAID: a buyer drawn to the Signature Collection generally is someone who wants a heated, fitted, offsite-built annexe delivered turnkey rather than a shell to finish, who is budgeting separately for groundworks and services, and who expects a planning conversation rather than an exemption where the building carries a kitchen and bathroom. WHAT THIS PARTICULAR BUYER MUST DO FIRST: ask the supplier which model the /signature-48/ page actually sells, obtain a dimensioned drawing, and get the delivery charge quantified against the GBP 47,650 'plus delivery' figure. Until then no purchasing decision rests on anything Atlas can certify.

Someone housing a family member, creating a long-stay guest annexe or adding rentable accommodation — not someone buying a garden office. They want a building that arrives heated, fitted with a kitchen and a bathroom and finished to a single price, and they have the site and the budget to treat services and groundworks as a separate project. They are prepared to go through a planning application rather than rely on an exemption, and to obtain a DIMENSIONED DRAWING before any other conversation, because the model numeral tells them nothing about the footprint. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone wanting an incidental garden room, since the use test excludes habitation; anyone in the Republic of Ireland who needs delivery confirmed today, as cross-border coverage is unconfirmed; anyone who needs a U-value to model running cost on a building of this size.

Someone building a second home on their own site — family accommodation, a long-term let, or a downsizing move within the same plot — who wants the building itself to arrive complete rather than to run a construction project. They accept that groundworks, drainage, water and power are a separate job, and they expect to apply for planning rather than rely on an exemption, because a kitchen and a bathroom put the use outside 'incidental'. They will get a dimensioned drawing and a written installation scope before signing, and a Republic of Ireland buyer will confirm cross-border delivery, installation and VAT treatment in writing first. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone wanting a garden office or studio — wrong scale and wrong specification; anyone depending on exempted development; anyone who needs published U-values to model running cost before committing at this size.

A buyer commissioning a second dwelling on their own land — multigenerational family accommodation, a long-term let, or a replacement for building an extension. They have the site area, they expect to make a planning application rather than rely on an exemption, and they are budgeting separately for foundations, water, drainage and power. What draws them to this supplier is that the building itself arrives finished: heated, wired, lit, kitchen and bathroom fitted, at one stated price. They will insist on a dimensioned drawing and a written installation scope before signing, and if they are in the Republic they will get cross-border delivery, installation and VAT treatment confirmed in writing first. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone wanting a garden office or studio, for whom this scale is wrong in every respect; anyone relying on exempted development; anyone who needs published thermal performance before committing to a building this size.

A homeowner with substantial site space and a six-figure budget solving a housing problem rather than a workspace one — typically accommodating adult children or ageing parents, or adding a long-term rental unit. Expects to run a planning application and a services connection alongside the purchase, and values a fixed offsite build and a 10-week programme over a traditional extension.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS THE BUILDING TO LOOK LIKE A SMALL HOUSE RATHER THAN A BOX. A pitched roof reads as traditional and sits comfortably in an older garden, and the extra ridge height gives a more generous feeling inside. They are choosing on appearance and volume, and they are comfortable dealing directly with a shed maker for the details. THEY MUST ASK ABOUT THE ROOF COVERING, because that single answer moves the applicable height limit between 3 m and 4 m. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs certainty on paper before enquiring.

A FAMILY REPLACING AN OLD SHED WITH SOMETHING THAT ALSO WORKS AS A ROOM. They have one usable spot in the garden and cannot afford to spend it twice, so a combined building is the practical answer. They tend to be pragmatic buyers who value storage as much as workspace and are happy with a traditional pitched-roof appearance. THEY NEED TO ASK FOR THE WHOLE FOOTPRINT, not the room size, because that is what the allowance measures. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants maximum working floor for the money, since a share of the building is storage.

A PRACTICAL BUYER DEALING WITH A LOCAL SHED MAKER RATHER THAN A BROCHURE. Someone who will telephone, describe the space they have, and take the sizes from the conversation — which is how a good deal of this market still works. They are choosing a pent roof because the garden is overlooked or the boundary is close. THEY WILL HAVE TO GATHER THE FIGURES THEMSELVES, because none is published. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing products on a spreadsheet, since this record can contribute no numbers to it.

SOMEONE SOLVING TWO PROBLEMS WITH ONE BUILDING IN A TIGHT GARDEN. They need a workspace and they need somewhere for the tools, the bikes and the mower, and they have one corner to put it in — close to a boundary or under a neighbour's windows, which is why the low pent roof matters. They are pragmatic, local-supplier buyers who will get the sizes by asking. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants the largest possible working room for the money, or one who needs published figures before making contact.

SOMEONE ATTRACTED TO THE BLACK CONTEMPORARY BOX WHO SHOULD BE WORKING FROM THE PUBLISHED SIZE LADDER INSTEAD OF THIS ENTRY. The XS at 5 m2 suits a single-desk pod; the M at 8.2 m2 adds a second room; the L at 9.5 m2 and Natural XL at 10.6 m2 give more open floor. ALL OF THEM ARRIVE UNINSULATED. NOT FOR: any buyer ordering from this record as it stands, since the variant it names does not exist in the supplier's catalogue.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A CONTEMPORARY BLACK BOX RATHER THAN A LOG CABIN, AND NEEDS TWO SEPARATE SPACES. The Astel Garden R-line styling and the 70 mm profile suit a modern house, and the two-room plan works for a use that needs a private corner — a treatment room and a waiting space, an office and a store. THEY MUST BUDGET FOR INSULATION on top of the EUR 7,769. NOT FOR: a single open workspace, where the same area in one room goes further; nor for a buyer who reads 'Office' in the name as meaning winter-ready.

A CITY HOUSEHOLD WITH A COURTYARD OR SMALL GARDEN AND NOWHERE TO PUT THINGS. Eight square metres under a flat roof takes bikes, tools and garden furniture and looks deliberate rather than temporary, which is the whole argument for a timber store over a metal one. THEY ARE COMPARING IT AGAINST OTHER SHEDS, correctly. NOT FOR: a workspace of any kind; nor for a buyer who has been shown both this and the Sacramento and believes they are choosing between two designs.

SOMEONE WITH A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN AND A REQUIREMENT THAT GENUINELY NEEDS 26 m2. A studio, a workshop, or a room serving several members of the household at once — and no shed, no bike store and no intention of adding one, because this building takes almost the entire allowance. THEY ARE ALSO A BUYER WHO BENEFITS DIRECTLY FROM THE 2026 CHANGE, which is worth knowing when comparing older online advice. NOT FOR: any plot with an existing structure over 3.82 m2; nor for a buyer who wants margin for error — the Nova at 22.5 m2 is the sensible retreat.

A HOUSEHOLD WHOSE GARDEN ROOM HAS TO DO TWO JOBS. Two people working on alternating days, or an office that becomes a gym or family room in the evening — the requirement that justifies 22.5 m2 rather than 18.7 m2. They have a reasonably large garden with at most a small shed in it, and they want a published area rather than a promise. NOT FOR: a plot already carrying a garage or a large shed, where 7.5 m2 of remaining allowance will not absorb it; nor for overnight accommodation.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A REAL ROOM WITHOUT A PLANNING CONVERSATION. Home office, gym or hobby space, in a garden that may already hold a shed — and 11.3 m2 of remaining allowance means that shed is unlikely to matter. They value a published area they can check themselves and an Irish supplier they can contact. THEIR REMAINING QUESTIONS ARE HEIGHT AND INSULATION, neither of which the catalogue answers. NOT FOR: overnight or guest use, which is a different consent route; nor for a household wanting to add a further structure later as well, where the arithmetic gets tighter.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH VISITING FAMILY AND NO SPARE BEDROOM, WHO UNDERSTAND THIS IS A CONSENT PROJECT. The fabric specification — 150 mm walls, insulated ceiling, Kingspan floor, radon barrier and DPC — is built for people sleeping in it, and that is the right specification for the brief. WHAT THEY MUST DO FIRST IS ESTABLISH THE ROUTE: Class 3 is unavailable on use, and Class 3A carries a 32 m2 minimum. NOT FOR: anyone assuming a garden building can simply become a bedroom; nor for a buyer who needs the planning answer from a website.

SOMEONE TRAINING SERIOUSLY ENOUGH THAT THE FLOOR AND THE CEILING BOTH MATTER. A Dublin or Leinster household putting real equipment into a garden building, who wants the foundations designed rather than guessed and the power installed rather than added later — and who will use the free site visit to settle the clear height. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the specification and dimensions from a website; nor for anyone whose training needs a published ceiling height before they will commit.

A homeowner with a broadly square area of garden to give over, few existing outbuildings, comfortable arranging base and assembly, wanting a compact single room for seasonal use, and budgeting around EUR 8,100 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a clear garden and no existing outbuildings, willing to give the whole statutory allowance to one structure, wanting a 14.5 m2 room for seasonal use, comfortable arranging base and assembly across a 592 x 502 cm envelope, and budgeting around EUR 8,700 at the current reduced price before groundworks.

SOMEONE WHOSE WORK DEPENDS ON THE ROOM AND WHO WANTS ONE CONTRACTOR TO DELIVER ALL OF IT. A Dublin household replacing a spare bedroom with a properly insulated, plastered, wired and heated office — and who values acoustic performance because they are on calls all day. THEY WILL HAVE A FREE SITE VISIT and should use it to settle the two things the website cannot: the footprint and the guarantee. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs to compare specifications online before making contact, since nothing measurable is readable; nor for anyone who requires a written warranty before committing.

A HOUSEHOLD WORKING THROUGH A LONG PRODUCT LIST AND NARROWING BY LOOK. With four contemporary models offering the same published information — none — the decision comes down to photographs and price, which is how most garden buildings are actually bought and why the missing dimensions matter. THEY WANT A MODERN ROOM AT AN ORDINARY SIZE, the commonest requirement there is. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs to demonstrate exemption compliance before ordering; nor for one who needs a large room, where the Roberta is the intended model.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden or a boundary run of about 7 m, wanting a summer room approaching 10 m2 with sheltered seating attached, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 7,250 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden or a boundary run of about 6 m, wanting a small summer room with sheltered seating attached, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 6,530 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a large garden and a long boundary run, prepared to check the planning position with their local authority before ordering, wanting the most enclosed room available for the money, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 7,580 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a large garden able to accommodate a 34 m2 envelope, prepared to seek planning permission, prioritising the supplier's thickest wall specification, willing to question the supplier closely about what the published footprint contains, and budgeting around EUR 13,610 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A MODERN HOUSE AND AN ORDINARY REQUIREMENT. One room, contemporary lines, nothing exotic — and a preference for a building that looks deliberate beside a modern extension rather than like a shed. THEY ARE CHOOSING BETWEEN FOUR SIMILAR-LOOKING MODELS, which is where a supplier conversation replaces the catalogue. NOT FOR: a period property, where the range's traditional summer-house forms sit better; nor for a buyer needing a large room, where the Large Modern Garden Room Roberta is the intended model.

A GOLFER WITH A GARDEN AND A SPECIFIC, MEASURABLE REQUIREMENT. This is not a garden room that happens to fit a simulator — it is designed around one, in a different panel system from the rest of the range, and that focus is the reason to choose it. THEY WILL BE MEASURING SWING CLEARANCE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, and the free site visit is where that gets settled. NOT FOR: a general workspace buyer, where the Office and Modular records are the intended products; nor for anyone who cannot get the internal height confirmed in writing.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS A ROOM DELIVERED FINISHED AND IS HAPPY TO START WITH A SITE VISIT RATHER THAN A CATALOGUE. Modular configuration plus a plastered, wired and lit handover means the buyer describes what they need and receives something usable — which suits people who do not want to manage trades. THEY ARE IN DUBLIN OR LEINSTER, where this supplier operates. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to compare specifications and sizes online first, since none is readable; nor for anyone who needs a written warranty before committing.

A homeowner with a boundary run of about 6 m, wanting a 16 m2 room in the thickest available wall with a small amount of built-in storage, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 12,400 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a large garden able to accommodate a 39 m2 structure, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting to consolidate a substantial room and storage into one building rather than two, and budgeting around EUR 12,750 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a large open garden able to accommodate a 46 m2 structure, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting substantial covered outdoor entertaining space alongside a 22 m2 room, and budgeting around EUR 15,330 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WITH A SPECIFIC BRIEF AND AN AWKWARD GARDEN. A homeowner who already knows roughly what they need the room to do, has measured the space available, and would rather have the building sized to fit than pick the nearest catalogue model. They are comfortable running a specification conversation and reading a quotation carefully, because that is where the detail lives. THEY SHOULD BE THE KIND OF BUYER WHO DOES THE ARITHMETIC FIRST: this range only rewards someone who totals their existing garden structures before choosing a size, because the upper end of the band leaves nothing in reserve. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to compare published specifications side by side, since none are held for this record.

SOMEONE BUILDING A YEAR-ROUND ROOM ON A TIGHT OR AWKWARD PLOT. They want the building warm enough to use in January, they have a specific footprint in mind because the garden dictates it, and they are prepared to work through a design conversation rather than pick a model number. They are the kind of buyer who asks what the panels are made of and how thick they are — and they will need to, because Atlas holds the system name but not the numbers. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing published prices and sizes across three suppliers this week, because this record offers neither; or anyone who wants the reassurance of a fixed, repeatable product with a known specification sheet.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A SMART SUMMER HOUSE WITH A SEATING TERRACE, NOT AN OFFICE. Eight and a half square metres of flat-roofed timber with a covered strip in front is a pleasant thing to have at the end of a garden, and at this price and specification that is what it is. THEY MAY LATER TAKE THE 44 mm AND DOUBLE-GLAZING UPGRADE and add insulation, at which point the supplier's own conditional wording is satisfied. NOT FOR: a daily workspace as supplied — the manufacturer itself says so; nor for a buyer expecting 11 m2 of room from the headline dimensions.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A DURABLE SINGLE-PURPOSE ROOM AND DOES NOT WANT TO MAINTAIN IT. A home office, a hobby room or a well-built store — chosen partly because steel does not need the annual attention timber does, from an Irish manufacturer. THEY HAVE A SMALL GARDEN OR OTHER PLANS FOR IT, since this model deliberately leaves most of the allowance unused. THEY SHOULD ASK ABOUT INSULATION EARLY, because that is the question steel raises and timber does not. NOT FOR: two occupants or equipment as well as a desk — the 3m x 4.2m at 12.60 m2 is the next step.

A HYBRID WORKER WITH AN EXISTING SHED THEY INTEND TO KEEP. That is the specific advantage of this size: 17 m2 of remaining allowance means the shed is not a problem, whereas the larger Adman models would make it one. They want a durable, low-maintenance building from an Irish manufacturer and are comfortable ordering from a published size list. THEIR ONE OPEN QUESTION IS THE ENVELOPE, since steel needs its insulation specified rather than assumed. NOT FOR: a room that must serve two people or double as a gym — that needs 4 m of depth, which begins at the 4m x 4.2m model.

A HOUSEHOLD WHOSE GARDEN IS LONG AND NARROW AND WHOSE REQUIREMENT IS LINEAR. A desk and a workbench, or an office with a storage end — uses that arrange naturally along a wall. They want the building to sit against a boundary rather than in the middle of the lawn, and they value steel's low maintenance. THEY STILL HAVE 14 m2 OF ALLOWANCE, so an existing shed is not a problem. NOT FOR: a gym, a studio, or two people working simultaneously — all of which need floor in front of the furniture, which 3 m of depth does not provide.

SOMEONE COMBINING TWO FUNCTIONS THAT DO NOT NEED TO SHARE FLOOR. An office at one end and a workshop or store at the other, separated by length rather than by a wall — a common requirement, and one this shape serves better than a square room of the same area. They have a long garden and a clear boundary run. NOT FOR: a household with an existing shed AND future plans for another structure, since 11 m2 will not cover both; nor for a use needing open central floor.

SOMEONE WITH A LONG BOUNDARY, AN EMPTY GARDEN AND A LINEAR REQUIREMENT. A workshop with a bench along one wall, a store combined with an office, or a series of separate uses arranged end to end — the brief this shape actually suits. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST EXPOSED TO A MEASUREMENT SURPRISE, because under 2.40 m2 of margin leaves nothing to absorb the difference between a designation and a measured footprint. NOT FOR: any plot with an existing structure; nor for a use needing open floor, where 3 m of depth defeats the area entirely.

An Irish homeowner at around the EUR 13k mark who wants two uses out of one building and values never having to re-treat or repaint it. Suits family homes needing a home office plus a gym, playroom or store. Less suited to someone wanting a single large open-plan studio, or to heavy year-round use where insulation depth matters most.

A HOUSEHOLD WHERE THE GARDEN ROOM IS DOING REAL WORK FOR SEVERAL PEOPLE. Two adults working from home, or a workspace that becomes a gym or family room outside office hours — requirements that need floor in the middle, not just along the walls. They have a reasonably large garden, and they are prepared to treat this building as the main structure in it. NOT FOR: a plot with a garage, where under 10 m2 of remaining allowance will not absorb it; nor for a buyer unwilling to ask for a dimensioned plan at this scale.

SOMEONE WITH A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN AND A REQUIREMENT THAT GENUINELY NEEDS 25 m2. A workshop, a studio, or a room serving several members of the household — and no shed, no garage and no plans for either, because this building effectively takes the allowance. THEY MUST BE WILLING TO ASK FOR A DIMENSIONED PLAN, since the certified layers record that the published designation is not a measured footprint and the margin here is too thin to absorb the difference. NOT FOR: any plot with an existing structure; nor for a buyer who wants to order from a size list without verification.

SOMEONE WHOSE REQUIREMENT HONESTLY EXCEEDS WHAT EXEMPTED DEVELOPMENT ALLOWS — a home business, a serious workshop, a building serving several people at once — and who has accepted a planning application as part of the project. THAT IS A REASONABLE POSITION; the failure mode is arriving at it by accident after ordering. THEY HAVE A LARGE SITE and are likely working with a designer already. NOT FOR: anyone relying on the exemption at any garden size, since this product is over the limit on its own published designation; nor for a buyer wanting a delivered product rather than a project.

A DESIGN-AWARE REMOTE WORKER WHO LIKES BUYING ONLINE. Someone comfortable specifying a building through a configurator rather than a showroom, who wants a clean open-plan room for one purpose, and who values knowing the exact area before making contact. They are not looking for a multi-use family space — 9.75 m2 is a single room — and they are choosing on clarity and form rather than on maximum square metres. THEY MUST BE WILLING TO PROJECT-MANAGE THE IRISH SIDE: with no published Irish installation route, the base, the delivery and the assembly are likely to be their responsibility to arrange and coordinate. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a local supplier to handle everything, or one who needs published U-values and a warranty before committing.

A HOUSEHOLD WHERE TWO PEOPLE, OR TWO ACTIVITIES, NEED THE SAME BUILDING. Two remote workers sharing a room, or one worker who also wants space for training or a hobby. They have decided that a single-desk pod will not last them, and they want the extra area without going near the planning threshold. THEY LIKE A SPECIFICATION THEY CAN REASON ABOUT: the exact doubling from the Base appeals to the kind of buyer who wants to understand what they are paying for, and who will happily use a configurator instead of a showroom. THEY MUST ACCEPT PROJECT RESPONSIBILITY IN IRELAND: with no published Irish installation route, base, delivery and assembly are likely theirs to organise. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a turnkey local supplier or documented thermal performance.

SOMEONE BUILDING AN OUTDOOR KITCHEN OR A LARGE COVERED STORE, NOT AN OFFICE. That is what the manufacturer sells this model for, and it is a genuine and under-served brief — a big, simple, low-profile timber building for cooking, entertaining and keeping things out of the weather. THEY WILL BE SELF-BUILDING and will already have a base. NOT FOR: anyone looking for a garden office or a year-round room — the 28 mm wall and the manufacturer's own use listing both rule it out.

A CAPABLE SELF-BUILDER WHO WANTS A LARGE SUMMER WORKSHOP AND WILL ARRANGE THE REST. Lasita sells timber and nothing else, so the buyer who does well here already has a base sorted and either the skills or a builder lined up — and accepts that the room will be a spring-to-autumn space unless they insulate the walls themselves. THEY VALUE THE PUBLISHED FIGURES, which are the most complete of any supplier in the catalogue. NOT FOR: a homeowner wanting a turnkey year-round office; nor for anyone who needs a confirmed Irish delivery and warranty route before ordering.

A HOUSEHOLD WANTING THE LARGEST EXEMPT BUILDING IT CAN GET FROM AN IRISH SUPPLIER WITH SHOWROOMS. Twenty-seven square metres is a substantial room, and the fact that it became exempt only in July 2026 is exactly why it is worth knowing about now. THEY WILL HAVE A CLEAR GARDEN, because 3 m2 of margin does not accommodate a shed. THEY SHOULD BE PLANNING SEASONAL OR UPGRADED USE, given the uninsulated specification. NOT FOR: a plot with existing structures; nor for a daily winter workspace without addressing the walls.

SOMEONE BUYING A SUMMER ROOM AND SAYING SO. A studio, a hobby space, a seasonal office, a garden sitting room — uses where four to five uncomfortable months a year are acceptable because the room will not be used in them. THEY ARE SPENDING LESS DELIBERATELY, not by accident. NOT FOR: a daily year-round workspace, where the insulated OAK or the High-Quality Insulation Office are the correct products and must be chosen at order; nor for a buyer who assumes they can add insulation later — at this supplier they cannot.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING A PROPER YEAR-ROUND OFFICE AND WILLING TO SPECIFY IT PROPERLY. Pineca rewards a buyer who engages with the four-tier ladder and penalises one who does not, because the class cannot be changed afterwards — and 18 m2 with 12 m2 of allowance to spare is a sensible size for a working room on an ordinary plot. THEY ARE COMPARING INSULATED AGAINST INSULATED, correctly. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to order from a model name without a specification conversation; nor for one expecting to upgrade the insulation later.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A NOISE PROBLEM AND A REAL BUDGET. Someone whose teenager drums, who records at home, or who teaches music and cannot keep doing it in the house — and who understands that acoustic isolation is expensive because it means building twice. At GBP 34,992 for the smallest 3 m x 4 m option, this is a specialist purchase, not a garden-office upgrade, and the buyer is choosing it for one function rather than for general flexibility. THEY ALSO NEED TO ACCEPT LESS ROOM THAN THE LABEL SUGGESTS: the isolated inner shell and the entrance lobby both eat into the space they are paying for. NOT FOR: a homeowner in the Republic of Ireland or Northern Ireland on current evidence, because no purchasing route is published for either.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A TIMBER CABIN FOR ITS OWN SAKE — the look, the smell of the wood, the traditional build — rather than the most efficient enclosure per euro. They are usually flexible on exact size, which is fortunate, because none is published; and they are buying from a retailer rather than commissioning a design. THEY MUST STILL DO THE MEASUREMENT WORK THEMSELVES, since this supplier's own catalogue shows how easily the internal-versus-external question decides an exemption. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs to confirm compliance before enquiring; nor for a garden already close to the combined 30 m2.

A homeowner wanting a garden building with a separated sleeping room — typically for occasional guests — who understands that overnight accommodation falls outside the exemption and that the footprint is too small for the Class 3A route, is prepared to seek planning permission and arrange services, and is budgeting around EUR 15,500 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WITH A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN AND A REQUIREMENT THAT GENUINELY NEEDS 30 m2 — a workshop, a studio with storage, a multi-use family room. They have no shed, no garage in the back garden and no plans for one, because this product uses the entire allowance. THEY ALSO NEED TO BE THE KIND OF BUYER WHO WILL ASK THE MEASUREMENT-BASIS QUESTION and wait for a written answer, since the whole exemption turns on it. NOT FOR: a garden with existing structures, where the combined total is breached immediately; nor for a buyer who wants margin for error; nor for habitation, which the exemption excludes at any size.

SOMEONE BUILDING A GARDEN PAVILION ON A LARGE PLOT, WITH A PLANNING APPLICATION IN PROSPECT. The covered area is the reason to choose this rather than a plain cabin, and buyers who want that should go in knowing the structure is not exempt and that the published height figures contradict each other. THEY ARE SELF-BUILDING and comfortable putting questions to the manufacturer. NOT FOR: any buyer relying on the exemption; nor for anyone who will not chase the height discrepancy before ordering.

A homeowner who wants a large single-space room in the thickest available wall and who will telephone or email the supplier to obtain written external dimensions and a confirmed room area before committing, since the published figures contradict one another. Budget around EUR 13,440 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A FIRST-TIME GARDEN-ROOM BUYER WHO WANTS THE DECISION TO BE SIMPLE. Sixteen square metres is enough for a real office, small enough that the exemption is never in doubt, and square enough to rearrange — which is what most households actually want and rarely say. THEY WILL BE COMPARING PRICES ACROSS SUPPLIERS, which is precisely where the missing wall class will mislead them. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs two distinct uses in one building; nor for anyone comparing headline prices without confirming what construction each one refers to.

THE MAINSTREAM GARDEN-ROOM BUYER: one household, one room, one use, an ordinary garden and no appetite for a planning conversation. Twenty square metres with ten to spare removes almost every risk from the purchase except the one the catalogue leaves open, which is what the walls are made of. THEY WILL LIKELY WORK IN IT FIVE DAYS A WEEK. NOT FOR: a buyer needing a divided or dual-use building, where the 6 × 4 m or 7 × 4 m give more length; nor for anyone unwilling to pin down the wall class.

ONE PERSON, ONE DESK, AND A GARDEN THEY DO NOT WANT TO GIVE UP. This is the size most people actually need rather than the size they first ask about, and the 15 m2 of remaining allowance means they are not foreclosing anything by choosing it. THEY OFTEN HAVE A SHED THEY INTEND TO KEEP. NOT FOR: a household wanting an office plus a gym or a guest space, where 3 m of depth cannot support two uses; nor for a buyer who needs the wall class settled from the website.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH AN ORDINARY SUBURBAN GARDEN THAT ALREADY HAS A SHED. That is the majority case, and it is exactly the case this size is built for — 24 m2 of room with 6 m2 left over is the arithmetic most buyers actually need. THEY WILL BE WORKING IN IT REGULARLY, so the unstated insulation class is the question they must resolve. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants to order from the website without a specification conversation; nor for one needing a room over 25 m2, where the margin disappears.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT HAS OUTGROWN THE IDEA OF A GARDEN OFFICE AND WANTS A GARDEN BUILDING. Two people working, or an office plus a studio, or a room that takes a sofa as well as a desk — 28 m2 supports all of it. THEY NEED A CLEAR GARDEN AND A WILLINGNESS TO PIN DOWN THE SPECIFICATION, because the model name settles neither the walls nor the price. NOT FOR: a plot with an existing shed, where the 2 m2 margin disappears; nor for a buyer who wants a turnkey installed figure without asking for one.

ONE PERSON WHO NEEDS A DOOR TO CLOSE. A small garden, a small budget, a laptop and a need to be out of the house for a few hours a day — that is what a 4 m2 pod solves, and it solves it without touching the planning allowance in any meaningful way. THEY MAY ALSO HAVE A GARDEN THAT SIMPLY WILL NOT TAKE A LARGER BUILDING. NOT FOR: anyone with equipment, files, a second monitor setup that needs depth, or an expectation of sitting in it comfortably through winter without a confirmed insulated specification.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A MODERN HOUSE AND A GARDEN THAT ALREADY HAS THINGS IN IT. The generous allowance margin is the practical advantage here, and the low-pitch roof with full front glazing suits a contemporary setting better than the range's more traditional forms. THEY WILL BE USING IT AS AN OFFICE, which is exactly why the insulation question has to be settled before ordering rather than after. NOT FOR: a buyer who takes the 'year-round' description at face value; nor for anyone needing the largest possible room, where the Nila and Laura go further.

A CONTINENTAL BUYER WANTING A SMALL, MODERN GARDEN BUILDING. Clean lines, a single-slope roof, an entry-level size — a mainstream choice in the markets Bertilo's shipping reaches. FOR AN IRISH READER, the value of this record is diagnostic rather than practical: it explains why a product that appears in searches cannot be bought here, and what the roof form would mean for the height limit if it could. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner wanting a delivered building; nor for anyone needing a defensible area figure.

SOMEONE WORKING UP A RANGE FROM THE ENTRY MODEL. They have decided on the pent-roofed modern form and are looking for a slightly larger version — the most common way a buyer moves through a product line, and the one this catalogue can least support, since the numerals establish nothing.
