FOR A CONTINENTAL BUYER the range is at least reachable. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published; nor for anyone who needs the size confirmed before enquiring.

A BUYER WHO TAKES THE UPGRADE BECAUSE IT IS OFFERED. That is the honest characterisation: with no published content, the Plus tier is chosen on the assumption that more is better, and the catalogue provides nothing to test that assumption. THE USEFUL THING THIS RECORD CAN DO is prompt the question the buyer would otherwise skip. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for anyone comparing on value, where an unpriced, undescribed upgrade cannot be assessed at all.

A HOUSEHOLD NEEDING A ROOM RATHER THAN A RETREAT — space for a desk and something else, in a form that suits a modern house. They are moving up a range on the assumption that the numbers mean something, which is the assumption this record exists to qualify. FOR A CONTINENTAL BUYER the line is reachable and the choice real. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a garden near its allowance, where an unmeasured mid-to-large model is a poor bet.

A BUYER WHO WANTS A PROPER ROOM AND THE BETTER SPECIFICATION, WITHOUT PAYING FOR THE LARGEST MODEL. That instinct is sound in most ranges; here it rests on two words the catalogue cannot define, which is why the enquiry matters more than the comparison. FOR A CONTINENTAL BUYER the product is reachable and a showroom or a drawing would settle it. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for anyone judging value from published information alone.

A CONTINENTAL BUYER WANTING THE LARGEST CONTEMPORARY MODEL IN THE LINE — a full room rather than a study, in a form that suits a modern house and a boundary site. THEY HAVE A LARGE GARDEN AND ACCESS TO THE SUPPLY CHAIN, which is what makes the product real for them and theoretical for an Irish reader. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published; nor for anyone whose priority is a defensible exemption position, which needs a measured footprint this line does not provide.

SOMEONE BUYING THE BEST VERSION OF A RANGE THEY HAVE ALREADY CHOSEN. A large contemporary garden room, fully specified, from a manufacturer they trust — and a budget that makes the top of the line the obvious pick. THAT BUYER IS ALSO THE ONE MOST EXPOSED to two undefined designations, which is worth saying plainly at the point where the most is being spent. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for a buyer who expects a catalogue to justify the premium.

A DAILY HOME WORKER WHO WANTS A CONTEMPORARY BUILDING AND AN INTERIOR THAT ARRIVES SOLVED. They are not fitting out a shell; they want an office-ready room with the light coming from the right direction. THE THERMAL QUESTION IS THEIR REAL ONE, because a garden office used five days a week through an Irish winter is only as good as its insulation — and nothing here is published. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a business receiving clients, where the incidental-use condition becomes live.

A POOL OWNER WITH A CONTEMPORARY HOUSE AND A TIDY SITE. They want the poolside building to look considered rather than utilitarian, which is what the pent form offers, and they need somewhere for changing, towels and equipment. THE GARDEN IS ALREADY DEVELOPED, which is precisely why the combined allowance is the question they most need to ask. NOT FOR: a household without a pool, where a general-purpose room serves better; nor for an Irish buyer, on availability grounds.

TWO PEOPLE WORKING FROM HOME IN A CONTEMPORARY HOUSE. Two desks, shared storage, a room that has to function all day and look right beside the house — the brief that leads to the top of an office line rather than the middle. THEY WILL BE THE HEAVIEST USERS OF THE BUILDING and therefore the most affected by the unpublished thermal specification. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a small garden, where the largest undimensioned model in a range is the least defensible choice.

A FAMILY WITH A POOL THAT GETS HEAVY USE. Children, visitors, towels, inflatables and equipment — a requirement the smaller poolhouse would not absorb, and the reason the larger model exists. THEY HAVE INVESTED HEAVILY IN THE GARDEN ALREADY, which makes the combined-allowance arithmetic both more important and more likely to have been overlooked. NOT FOR: a modest pool, where the Pentus 2 Poolhouse is proportionate; nor for an Irish buyer, on availability grounds; nor for a garden already at its limit.

SOMEONE WANTING A SIMPLE WORKSPACE POD WHO IS PREPARED TO ASK BASIC QUESTIONS FIRST. The use case is straightforward — a room at the end of the garden for work, study or a hobby — and that is a common and sensible requirement. What this buyer needs is not a design conversation but two or three factual answers the supplier has not published: how big is it, how tall is it, and what is it made of. THEY SHOULD NOT ASSUME THE MODEL NUMBER IS A SIZE. NOT FOR: anyone comparing products on square metres or cost per square metre today, because this record cannot contribute a figure to that comparison; or anyone who needs the room for sleeping, which is a different product and a different planning route.

A FAMILY CREATING INDEPENDENT SLEEPING SPACE — for an adult child, an elderly parent, or regular guests. The decision is driven by who will sleep there and for how long, and it carries obligations a garden-office buyer never meets: drainage, heating, fire safety, and a consent route that may involve formal notice to the planning authority. THE BUYER WHO SUCCEEDS HERE is one who accepts that from the outset and budgets for it, rather than discovering it after ordering. NOT FOR: someone who wants a workspace — the sister Pod 17 Studio is the record for that requirement, and it is not excluded on use; or anyone who assumes an overnight room in the garden is a simple purchase because it is small.

An ENGLISH homeowner who trains seriously at home — a rack, a bench, a treadmill or cross-trainer — and who knows that a garden gym stands or falls on two things most suppliers never mention: floor behaviour under load and internal clear height. They are here because Booths publishes both, and they will specify the extended 7 ft 10 in height rather than accept the 2,080 mm standard, because overhead pressing and skipping do not fit under it. They value that no concrete base is needed, that the floor is decoupled, and that the guarantee runs to 25 years. They will budget separately for the air-conditioning unit, mainly for its dehumidification, and they will confirm with the supplier WHICH MODEL they are being quoted, since no QC8 appears in the current range. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser — no Irish delivery is published and the supplier's planning claims are UK law; anyone who needs a U-value; anyone who would accept the standard height without checking it against their equipment.

A HYBRID OR FULL-TIME HOME WORKER WITH A CONVENTIONAL SETUP. A desk, a screen or two, a filing box and somewhere for a visitor to sit — and a garden that may already hold a shed, which at this size does not matter. They want a delivered building at a modest price rather than a designed one, and they are unlikely to need anything larger. THE QUESTION THEY SHOULD PRESS is what the walls are made of, since nothing about the envelope is published. NOT FOR: a gym, a studio, or two people working simultaneously.

SOMEONE WITH A SMALL GARDEN, A LAPTOP AND A NEED TO GET OUT OF THE KITCHEN. One or two days a week of calls and screen work, no equipment, no visitors — and a budget that rules out anything larger. THE GARDEN MAY ALREADY HOLD A SHED, which is precisely why this size suits them: the allowance is not a live question. NOT FOR: full-time work with printing, storage or two screens; nor for anyone who will want a gym or guest use later — the QC9 at about 7.43 m2 is the first size where a second function becomes plausible.

SOMEONE TRAINING AT HOME WHO HAS RUN OUT OF ROOM INDOORS. A weights bench, a bike or a mat and some floor — a modest setup rather than a full gym, which is what a compact-tier building implies. THEY CARE MORE ABOUT CLEAR HEIGHT THAN ABOUT SQUARE METRES, and they will find that neither figure is published, so the enquiry has to do the work the catalogue cannot. NOT FOR: a rack, a rower with a raised deck, or anything requiring confirmed ceiling clearance before purchase; nor for a buyer who wants to compare specifications before making contact.

SOMEONE WANTING A SMALL PRIVATE SPACE THAT IS NOT A WORKPLACE. A reader, a painter, someone who meditates, or a household member who simply needs a door between themselves and a busy house. The scale suits the purpose, and the low cost makes it a discretionary rather than a major purchase. THEY SHOULD BE HONEST WITH THEMSELVES ABOUT OVERNIGHT USE, because that is the line the exemption draws. NOT FOR: guest accommodation, which needs a different consent route entirely; nor for a working office with equipment, where even this much floor becomes restrictive.

A UK homeowner with a garden worth looking at — a mature planting scheme, a view, or a long lawn — who wants a studio that frames it. Typically a writer, designer, therapist or remote professional who spends long hours in the room and cares about natural light. Budget from around GBP 11,000 all-in, and willing to accept a slightly higher heat loss through the glazing in exchange for the outlook.

A UK homeowner in a terrace or townhouse with a courtyard-sized garden, who has run out of room indoors and needs one door they can close. Usually a single remote worker rather than a household sharing the space. Accepts paying a premium per square metre because the constraint is the site, not the budget, and wants the building insulated and wired properly rather than improvised.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE, and the ambiguity here is unusually consequential: a workspace buyer and a buyer housing a family member face different regulations, different service requirements and different budgets, and this record cannot tell them apart. THE ONE OBSERVATION AVAILABLE: whoever pursues it will be starting with a use conversation rather than a size conversation, and should not assume that a collection named for dwelling can be treated as a garden office.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE. A buyer drawn to the name is responding to positioning rather than to anything Atlas can verify, and no profile has been built from it. THE ONE OBSERVATION AVAILABLE: anyone approaching this supplier will be doing the specification work themselves in correspondence — model names, external footprints, heights, build-up and inclusions — which suits a patient buyer and not a comparison shopper.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE. THE ONLY OBSERVATION AVAILABLE: a buyer approaching this record is beginning a conversation with a manufacturer rather than choosing from a catalogue. They will need to establish the model list, the external footprints, the heights and what the price includes before they can compare anything — which suits someone unhurried and methodical, and does not suit a buyer trying to shortlist from published information this week.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A LARGE, HANDSOME TIMBER ROOM AND WILL SPECIFY THE INSULATION SEPARATELY. Twenty-two and a half square metres of verified internal floor with a full-width aluminium slider is a serious garden building, and the buyer who does well here treats the headline price as the shell price and budgets accordingly. THEY CAN VISIT LIMERICK OR WEXFORD to see it. NOT FOR: a buyer expecting a EUR 15,664 garden office to arrive winter-ready; nor for a plot already carrying a shed, where 6 m2 of remaining allowance will not stretch.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE. With no size, specification or price, any profile would be invented, and the modular-homes association is exactly the kind of shortcut this layer exists to refuse. THE ONE OBSERVATION THAT CAN BE MADE: a buyer approaching this supplier is entering a conversation, not a catalogue — they will be asking for model names, dimensions, build-up and inclusions from scratch, and they should also establish which of the two Atlas-recorded Rayco entities they are actually dealing with. That suits someone methodical and unhurried, and suits nobody who wants to compare three options this weekend.

A self-directed homeowner around EUR 9k-15k all-in who wants a properly insulated year-round room and is willing to project-manage base, assembly and electrics. Suits a home office with a meeting corner, a studio or a hobby room.

A confident, hands-on homeowner or self-builder who already has groundworks and an electrician arranged, and who would rather spend the budget on the building envelope than on a main contractor's margin. Comfortable managing a cross-border purchase and a self-assembly kit. Entirely wrong for anyone who wants one company, one price and one point of accountability.

A hands-on homeowner or self-builder with groundworks and an electrician already lined up, who would rather put the budget into the building envelope than into a main contractor's margin. Comfortable managing a cross-border purchase. Wrong for anyone who wants one company, one price and one point of accountability.

A value-driven, capable homeowner who has done the per-square-metre arithmetic and has a builder ready. Wants a large, warm, year-round room — home office plus gym, or a studio — for well under Irish turnkey money, and accepts owning the project management in exchange.

A homeowner with a large site building permanent independent accommodation — multigenerational living or a two-bed rental. Treats this as a house project with an architect, planner and contractor, and is choosing SIPS-House to keep the structural envelope cost down rather than to avoid using professionals.

A homeowner solving an accommodation problem — an adult child, an ageing parent, or a long-term rental — with substantial garden space and the appetite to run a planning application alongside the build. Expects to appoint a contractor rather than self-assemble, and is using the kit route to control the envelope cost of a project that is genuinely a small house.

A homeowner with a decent garden and a real project appetite, budgeting roughly EUR 13k-22k once base, electrics and assembly are added. Wants one large multi-purpose room rather than a compact office, and is comfortable coordinating trades themselves.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A LONG GARDEN, A BOUNDARY TO BUILD ALONG AND NO EXISTING OUTBUILDINGS. That is a specific combination, and it is the only one this product suits on the planning arithmetic. THEY USUALLY WANT TWO USES IN ONE BUILDING — a workspace and a gym, or an office and a workshop — which is what ten metres of run buys. THEY MUST BE WILLING TO CLEAR THE GARDEN OR APPLY FOR PERMISSION. NOT FOR: a plot that already holds a shed, where this size cannot be exempt; nor for a buyer who has not confirmed the insulation specification.

A CAREFUL BUYER WHO READS SPECIFICATIONS AND WANTS A ROOM THAT WORKS ALL YEAR. This is the Quick-Garden product that rewards that approach: the dimensions, the base size, the wall build-up and the warranty are all published, so the purchase can be planned properly rather than negotiated. THE 3 m DEPTH SUITS A BOUNDARY POSITION and gives a long, well-lit room. THEY MAY WELL SELF-BUILD, though twin-skin adds materially to the effort. NOT FOR: someone wanting a square plan; nor for a buyer unwilling to confirm which twin-skin class is being supplied.

SOMEONE WITH A SMALL CITY GARDEN AND A MOWER TO PUT SOMEWHERE. That is precisely the buyer the manufacturer describes, and a flat-roofed 8 m2 timber store is a considerable improvement on a metal shed in a garden that is looked at from the house. THEY WILL LAY IT ON AN EXISTING SLAB OR PATIO, which is why the optional floor matters. NOT FOR: any workspace use — no floor as standard, 28 mm walls and narrow lights make that a different product; nor for a buyer expecting the supplier to build it.

A FAMILY BUILDING A SHARED LEISURE ROOM RATHER THAN A PRIVATE OFFICE. Gym equipment at one end, a pool or table-tennis table at the other, teenagers using it in the evening — the requirement is floor area and clearance, and 31.20 m2 in a near-square plan delivers both. THEY ARE MAKING A LARGER, MORE PERMANENT INVESTMENT than a garden-office buyer, and the planning application should be treated as part of that project rather than as an obstacle to it. THEY NEED TO GO IN WITH EYES OPEN: this product cannot be made exempt by tidying the garden, and anyone promising otherwise is mistaken. NOT FOR: a buyer whose main objective is avoiding planning — the Shanette Home Gym at 24.80 m2 is the record for that.

SOMEONE TRAINING SERIOUSLY AT HOME AND TIRED OF DOING IT IN A GARAGE. They need depth as much as area — space to stand back from a rack, lay out a mat, or swing a kettlebell — and they have concluded that a small pod will not do. They are practical buyers who will happily deal with an established shed manufacturer rather than a design studio, and who care more about floor space and floor strength than about architecture. THEY MUST DO ONE PIECE OF HOMEWORK: with only about 5 m2 of allowance left over, an existing shed or garage needs measuring before ordering. NOT FOR: a garden that is already built up, or a buyer who needs documented insulation performance for year-round training in cold weather — none is held.

A HOMEOWNER IN AN ESTABLISHED SUBURB WITH A PERIOD OR TRADITIONAL HOUSE, who wants the garden room to look as though it belongs. They are as concerned with how the building sits beside the house and the neighbours as with the specification, and they value an Irish supplier who will visit before designing. THEY MAY ALSO BE THE BUYER WHO NEEDS EXTRA HEIGHT — for a room with a vaulted ceiling or a loft — in which case the tiled pitched roof is doing regulatory work as well as aesthetic work. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing published specifications online; nor for a contemporary flat-roofed design brief, which the Contemporary Range serves.

SOMEONE STARTING A CONVERSATION RATHER THAN PLACING AN ORDER. They want a modern-looking garden room, they have a budget rather than a specification, and they expect the supplier to size and design it around their garden — which is what a range-based Irish supplier is set up to do. THEY WILL GET THEIR PLANNING ANSWER DURING THAT PROCESS, not before it, and should insist it is written into the quotation. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing published specifications across suppliers before making contact, since there is nothing here to compare; nor for anyone who needs a fixed price from a website.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS THE TELEVISION OUT OF THE LIVING ROOM AND THE NOISE OUT OF THE HOUSE. Usually a family with teenagers, or a couple treating film as a hobby worth a room — they want an experience rather than extra workspace, and they are buying a design service from an Irish supplier rather than a flat-pack. THEY ARE ALSO LIKELY TO SPECIFY UPWARD as the design develops, which is exactly when the height limit becomes live. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs a multi-purpose room, since cinema fit-out works against daylight and flexibility; nor for anyone who needs published figures before committing.

A COMMITTED GOLFER WHO HAS PRICED A SIMULATOR AND DISCOVERED NOTHING IN THE HOUSE IS TALL ENOUGH. That is usually what brings someone to this product: the equipment budget is settled and the building is the obstacle. They have a garden with room and an Irish supplier who will survey it. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST EXPOSED TO A LATE PLANNING SURPRISE, because the height requirement is not negotiable once the simulator is chosen. NOT FOR: a casual player, for whom a net in a general-purpose room is a fraction of the cost; nor for a garden where a taller structure would dominate neighbours' outlook.

SOMEONE WHO ALREADY TRAINS AT HOME AND HAS RUN OUT OF PATIENCE WITH THE SPARE ROOM. They know that a bike in a sealed box gets unbearable within twenty minutes, which is why the ventilation matters to them more than the finish. Usually a committed cyclist or a household sharing one gym space, buying from an Irish supplier who will survey the site. THEY SHOULD TREAT HEIGHT AS THE FIRST QUESTION, not the last. NOT FOR: occasional use, where a general-purpose insulated room at a published size is cheaper and simpler; nor for a small garden with an existing shed already using the allowance.

A CAPABLE SELF-BUILDER WITH A MODEST BUDGET. Someone who has laid a base before, owns the tools and would rather spend a weekend than the installation fee — and who accepts that the finish will be theirs to get right. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST IN CONTROL OF THE PLANNING OUTCOME, since siting and finished height are decisions they make on the day. NOT FOR: a buyer expecting a delivered, installed, finished building; nor for a difficult or sloping site, where base preparation is the hardest part of a kit build.

A homeowner with a small or already-occupied garden and a limited budget, wanting a plain 9 m2 room for storage, a hobby or seasonal work, comfortable arranging a base and assembling a small kit themselves, and budgeting around EUR 5,170 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a courtyard or a garden already close to the statutory limit, needing a single-person work booth rather than a room, prepared to ask the supplier for the wall specification and confirmed dimensions before ordering and to arrange base, assembly and electrical connection separately, budgeting around EUR 6,200 for the delivered kit.

A homeowner wanting a single-person garden office on a medium plot, prepared to commission insulation advice and a certified electrical connection separately, willing to ask the supplier what the published envelope contains, and budgeting around EUR 7,320 for the delivered kit before groundworks and fit-out.

SOMEONE WITH A SMALL GARDEN OR A SMALL BUDGET — OFTEN BOTH. One desk, one purpose, and a preference for keeping most of the lawn and most of the allowance. THEY ARE ALSO THE HANSA24 BUYER LEAST EXPOSED to the range's missing dimensions, because at this scale the margin absorbs the uncertainty. NOT FOR: two occupants or a gym, where the larger models exist; nor for anyone who needs the room to store garden equipment as well, where the Barbados Plus or Super Tom layouts are the intended answer.

A homeowner with a small or already-occupied garden and a limited budget, wanting a simple enclosed room for seasonal use, comfortable arranging a base and assembling a light kit themselves, and budgeting around EUR 4,780 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with an open area of garden and few other outbuildings, wanting sheltered outdoor seating with a small enclosed room attached in a thicker-than-average wall, comfortable arranging base and assembly, and budgeting around EUR 10,230 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a medium garden and few other outbuildings who wants sheltered outdoor seating as the main purpose, accepts a small enclosed store rather than a working room, and is budgeting around EUR 9,110 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WITH A MODEST NOISE PROBLEM AND A LIMITED BUDGET FOR SOLVING IT. A singer, a podcaster, a hobby musician — someone who needs containment rather than a professional recording environment, and for whom the entry tier is likely to be sufficient. THEY ARE BUYING A FUNCTION, NOT FLOOR AREA, and should expect the usable interior to be small relative to the building. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on current evidence, as no purchasing route is published; nor for anyone whose real requirement is a general-purpose office, where the isolation cost buys nothing.

A REGULAR HOME MUSICIAN OR TEACHER RATHER THAN AN OCCASIONAL ONE. Someone playing or recording most weeks, whose household or neighbours have already noticed, and who wants the problem properly solved rather than softened. They will be choosing between tiers, which means they need the acoustic figures Atlas does not hold. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on current evidence; nor for a buyer who needs the room to double as a general workspace, since isolated construction costs usable floor.

SOMEONE WITH A LOUD INSTRUMENT AND CLOSE NEIGHBOURS. Drums, amplified guitar, brass — the cases where basic containment is not enough and the household has probably already had a conversation about it. They are prepared to pay for performance rather than space, and they should be asking for measured isolation figures. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on current evidence; nor for someone who assumes the higher tier also delivers a bigger room, which nothing published supports.

A WORKING MUSICIAN, PRODUCER OR TEACHER RUNNING A PRACTICE FROM HOME. The building is part of their livelihood rather than a hobby space, which changes the calculation: isolation performance and reliability matter more than cost per square metre, and they will expect measured figures. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO NEED A LARGE ROOM AND THE MOST EXPOSED TO THE ENVELOPE PENALTY, so the external footprint is a live question for them. NOT FOR: an Irish buyer on current evidence, nor a hobbyist for whom a lower tier would do.

A homeowner with a large open garden, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting a substantial room with a large covered veranda in a near-square plan, willing to ask the supplier what the premium over comparable models represents, and budgeting around EUR 19,290 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS TO STOP WORKING AT THE KITCHEN TABLE AND WANTS IT SOLVED IN ONE TRANSACTION. A 2 m pod delivered, built, wired and heated, with no builder to find and no base to pour, is about as low-friction as a garden building gets — and cedar cladding gives it a finish rather than a shed appearance. THEY HAVE A SMALL GARDEN AND A SINGLE OCCUPANT IN MIND. NOT FOR: anyone with equipment, storage or a second person to accommodate; nor for a buyer who needs a published footprint before committing.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A MODERN HOUSE AND NO APPETITE FOR RE-TREATING TIMBER. Black composite on a small pod reads as a considered addition rather than a shed, and a sliding door keeps the useful floor clear in a building where every metre counts. THEY WANT ONE ROOM, FINISHED, WITH NOBODY ELSE TO ORGANISE. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants natural timber that silvers with age, where the larch and cedar options are the answer; nor for anyone needing a published footprint first.

SOMEONE WHO WILL USE THE GARDEN AROUND THE POD, NOT JUST THE POD. A canopy gives somewhere to leave boots, stand out of the rain or sit with the doors open — small things that decide whether a garden building gets used in an Irish spring. THEY WANT A COMPACT WORKSPACE WITH A LITTLE SHELTER, and they are buying a finished, heated room rather than a shell. NOT FOR: a buyer trying to keep the roofed footprint to an absolute minimum, where the canopy works against them on the allowance.

SOMEONE WHO WILL SPEND HOURS IN A SMALL ROOM AND WANTS IT TO FEEL LIGHT. On a 3 m pod the difference between one opening and two is the difference between a box and a room, and that matters more than any specification a homeowner is likely to compare. THEY WANT NATURAL TIMBER AND A FINISHED, HEATED SPACE with nobody else to organise. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants sheltered outdoor space, where the canopy version is the answer; nor for anyone who needs storage built in, where the 4 m Room + Store is the intended model.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS THE ROOM TO BECOME PART OF THE GARDEN IN SUMMER. Bifolds are bought for that one effect, and they deliver it in a way French or sliding doors do not — a household that entertains, or works with the front open, gets real value from them. THEY ARE PAYING FOR GLASS AND IRONMONGERY AS MUCH AS FOR FLOOR AREA. NOT FOR: a north-facing or exposed position where a fully glazed front is a liability; nor for a buyer prioritising thermal performance, which is not quantified anywhere in this range.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING ONE ROOM FOR MIXED USE — work during the week, somewhere to sit at the weekend, doors open on the four warm days Ireland gets. French doors are bought for that second use, and a 4 m pod is big enough to support it without dominating the garden. THEY WANT THE WHOLE THING HANDLED: delivered, built, wired and heated by the supplier. NOT FOR: a boundary position where door swing is awkward, which is what the sliding and bifold versions solve.

A FAMILY REPLACING A TIRED SHED WITH SOMETHING THAT ALSO WORKS AS A ROOM. Bikes, mowers and garden tools have to live somewhere, and a household that removes the old shed and puts a room-plus-store in its place often ends up with more usable garden and a better allowance position than it started with. THEY VALUE TIDINESS AS MUCH AS WORKSPACE. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants the largest possible working room for the footprint, where a plain 4 m or 5 m pod gives more; nor for anyone storing anything that needs to stay dry and warm without confirming the store's specification.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS THE LOOK OF TIMBER WITHOUT THE ASSUMPTION OF UPKEEP. Composite is bought for that reason more than any other, and a 5 m room in a teak tone with French doors is a conventional, easy-to-live-with building. THEY MAY BE BUYING FOR A RENTAL, A SECOND HOME OR SIMPLY A BUSY HOUSEHOLD where re-treating timber will not happen. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants natural timber that silvers and ages; nor for one expecting the catalogue to prove the composite lasts longer, which it does not.

A PRACTICAL HOUSEHOLD BUYING A ROOM THEY DO NOT WANT TO THINK ABOUT AGAIN. Composite cladding and sliding doors are both chosen to reduce future effort, and the turnkey package removes the effort at the front end too — delivered, built, wired, heated. THEY ARE OFTEN SITING IT TIGHT TO A BOUNDARY, where a swinging door would not work. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants the room to open right up in summer, where the bifold configurations are the point; nor for anyone who wants natural timber.

SOMEONE WHOSE WORK NEEDS WALLS. A recording space, a painting studio, a therapy room, a home office with two screens and a shelf of files — all of them are better served by a mostly solid building than by a glass front, and this is the only 5 m configuration in the range that offers it. THEY MAY ALSO BE OVERLOOKED and want the privacy. NOT FOR: a household buying the room for the view or for summer entertaining, where the bifold and French-door versions are the point.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING A GARDEN ROOM AS MUCH FOR SUMMER AS FOR WORK. Five metres of bifold onto a lawn is a social space first and an office second, and buyers who want that should be honest with themselves about it — it is a perfectly good reason to buy. THEY WILL WANT A SOUTH OR WEST ASPECT and a level terrace outside the doors. NOT FOR: a shaded or wind-exposed position; nor for a buyer whose primary need is a warm, quiet, year-round workspace, where a less glazed configuration serves better.

A FAMILY THAT WANTS ANOTHER ROOM AND HAS THE GARDEN FOR IT. Five metres of timber-clad room with doors onto the lawn is the picture most people have in mind when they start looking, and this configuration is the plainest expression of it. THEY WANT IT DONE FOR THEM — delivered, built, wired, heated — which is exactly what this supplier sells. NOT FOR: a narrow garden or a boundary position where the doors cannot swing; nor for a household that already has a large shed and cannot risk an unpublished width.

A HOUSEHOLD ADDING A ROOM RATHER THAN AN OFFICE. At 5 m the building takes furniture, two people and a use that changes through the week — and the turnkey package means it arrives finished rather than as a project. THEY ARE OFTEN SITING IT ALONG A BOUNDARY, which is why the sliding doors matter. NOT FOR: a garden that already carries a large shed, where the unpublished width becomes a genuine exemption risk; nor for a buyer who will not chase the footprint figure.

SOMEONE WHO HAS DECIDED ON THE BUILDING AND IS NOW CHOOSING HOW IT LOOKS. That is the honest description of this record: the size, the doors and the package are settled, and the teak finish is the remaining decision. IT SUITS A DARKER OR MORE CONTEMPORARY GARDEN SCHEME than natural larch. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants the finish decision made on durability evidence, which this range does not publish for any cladding.

A FAMILY SOLVING TWO PROBLEMS WITH ONE BUILDING AND WANTING IT TO LOOK GOOD DOING IT. The room opens onto the garden for the family; the store takes the mower and the bikes out of sight. THAT IS A COMMON AND SENSIBLE BRIEF, and it is why this configuration exists. THEY ARE REPLACING BOTH A SHED AND A SPARE ROOM. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs every metre of the roofed footprint as working space; nor for a garden that is already close to the 30 m2 combined limit.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT WANTS THE GARDEN TO LOOK FINISHED. Bikes, tools and bins have to go somewhere, and hiding them inside the same building as the room is a tidier answer than a second structure — particularly on a plot where a shed would be visible from the house. THEY VALUE APPEARANCE AND ORDER as much as floor area. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs the maximum working room for the roofed footprint; nor for a plot where the combined allowance is already tight, since the store counts in full.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A CONTEMPORARY HOUSE AND A LARGE GARDEN, BUYING A SECOND LIVING SPACE. Black composite at six metres is a design decision as much as a practical one, and the households that choose it usually care how the garden looks as a whole. THEY WILL NOT WANT TO BE RE-TREATING TIMBER on a building this size. NOT FOR: a period property where a dark composite facade sits awkwardly; nor for a garden where 6 m cannot be accommodated within the allowance.

A FAMILY CLEARING THE GARDEN AND STARTING AGAIN. One building that replaces both the shed and the spare room, in a finish that will not need attention, on a plot large enough to take six metres — that is a coherent and increasingly common plan. THEY ARE REMOVING AN EXISTING STRUCTURE, which is also what makes the allowance arithmetic work. NOT FOR: a household keeping its existing shed, where this combination is very likely to breach the 30 m2 limit; nor for anyone ordering without the total footprint.

SOMEONE BUYING THE VIEW. A large plot, a garden worth looking at, and a household that wants a room to sit in as much as work in — this configuration exists for exactly that, and nothing else in the range does it as completely. THEY WILL SPEND MORE ON GLASS THAN ON FLOOR. NOT FOR: a screen-based workspace where glare is a daily problem; nor for an exposed or north-facing position; nor for a garden where the width risk cannot be resolved before ordering.

A HOUSEHOLD BUILDING A GARDEN ROOM AS A PROJECT RATHER THAN A PURCHASE. At six metres this is a significant building in a garden and a significant spend, usually made by a family with a large plot who want a second living space as much as a workspace. THEY WILL WANT A TERRACE OUTSIDE THE DOORS and a south or west aspect. NOT FOR: an ordinary suburban garden that already carries a shed, where the width risk is real; nor for a buyer who needs certainty on the exemption from published information.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS A WIDE OPENING WITHOUT THE COMPLEXITY OF BIFOLDS. A three-metre slider gives most of the effect with fewer moving parts and less to maintain, on a building large enough to take it — which suits a household that values the view but not the ironmongery. THEY ARE BUYING A SIGNIFICANT BUILDING and should treat it as such. NOT FOR: a small or already-built-on garden, where a 6 m unit is a poor fit; nor for a buyer who will not verify the building width before ordering.

A HOUSEHOLD REBUILDING THE BACK OF THE GARDEN IN ONE MOVE. The old shed goes, and a single seven-metre building takes its place holding a room, a store and everything that used to be scattered — which is a coherent plan and the only one on which the allowance arithmetic can work at this size. THEY HAVE A LARGE PLOT AND ARE CLEARING IT. NOT FOR: any garden keeping existing structures, where this configuration will very likely need planning permission; nor for a buyer who has not obtained the total footprint in writing.

A FAMILY BUYING THE BIGGEST TIMBER ROOM THE SUPPLIER MAKES, WITH A PROPER OPENING ONTO THE GARDEN. Three metres of French doors on a seven-metre building is a considered specification, usually chosen by households treating this as a second reception room rather than an office. THEY WILL HAVE A LARGE, LEVEL, LARGELY EMPTY GARDEN. NOT FOR: a plot with existing structures, where the combined allowance almost certainly rules this size out; nor for a buyer who reads the product name as a footprint.

SOMEONE WITH A CRAFT, A PRACTICE OR A BUSINESS RUN FROM HOME. Seven metres of wall and one good window is a workshop, a studio or a consulting room — uses that need equipment against walls and privacy from the garden, and that a glazed-front pod would serve badly. THEY HAVE THE PLOT AND THE PROGRAMME to justify the largest building in the range. NOT FOR: a household wanting a social garden room, where the bifold configurations exist; nor for a garden where 7 m cannot fit inside the allowance.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN AND A REAL PROGRAMME FOR THE BUILDING. Seven metres is not bought casually — it is bought by families who need two spaces, or a studio and an office, or a room that will take a table and chairs as well as a desk. THEY MUST HAVE A CLEAR PLOT, because the allowance leaves almost no room for anything else. NOT FOR: an ordinary suburban garden with an existing shed; nor for a buyer unwilling to establish the footprint before committing.

SOMEONE WHOSE WORK NEEDS FLOOR AREA IN THE MIDDLE OF THE ROOM. An artist, a maker, a yoga or movement practice, a photographer — uses where furniture goes to the walls and the centre stays clear, which is exactly what a nearly square plan provides and a long narrow one does not. THEY HAVE A LARGE, EMPTY GARDEN, because 5.6 m2 of remaining allowance leaves room for essentially nothing else. NOT FOR: a garden with any existing structure; nor for a buyer who wants margin for error, where the 5.0 m × 4.0 m at 20 m2 is the sensible retreat.

A FAMILY HOUSING ONE RELATIVE — USUALLY A PARENT WHO NEEDS INDEPENDENCE AND PROXIMITY AT THE SAME TIME, or an adult child who cannot find a rental. They are Dublin-based, dealing with a genuine housing problem rather than a lifestyle upgrade, and they need a kitchen and bathroom rather than a desk. THEY ARE ALSO ENTERING A PLANNING PROCESS, not buying a delivered product, and should budget time as well as money. NOT FOR: anyone hoping to avoid planning — that is the one thing this size does not deliver. NOT FOR two occupants; the larger models exist for that.

A FAMILY SOLVING A HOUSING PROBLEM RATHER THAN A SPACE PROBLEM. Typically a parent creating independent accommodation for an adult child, or an adult child creating it for a parent who needs to be close but not in the house. The decision is driven by who will live there, and the building follows. THEY NEED A HIGHER TOLERANCE FOR PROCESS THAN A GARDEN-OFFICE BUYER: services, drainage, fire and building standards and a consent route all come into play, and none of them applies to a workspace. THEY ALSO NEED TO BE COMFORTABLE ASKING FOR NUMBERS THE SUPPLIER HAS NOT PUBLISHED — the as-built area, the construction specification and what the quoted price actually covers, because Atlas holds a pricing page rather than a specification.

A homeowner with a deeper garden than boundary run, wanting a 9 m2 room with an outdoor terrace in front, willing to confirm with the supplier how the terrace is built and whether it is roofed, and budgeting around EUR 7,410 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long deep garden, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting a substantial room and covered veranda facing down the plot, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 14,560 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a medium garden and few other outbuildings who wants a large sheltered outdoor area as the main purpose, accepts a small enclosed store, and is budgeting around EUR 8,180 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a garden outlook worth opening onto, wanting a 19 m2 room in the thickest available wall with a full-width folding door set, prepared to arrange careful assembly and to question the supplier about glazing and door warranty, and budgeting around EUR 14,300 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a garden outlook worth opening onto, wanting a 19 m2 room in the thickest available wall with a full-width folding door set, prepared to arrange careful assembly and to question the supplier about glazing and door warranty, and budgeting around EUR 13,690 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a small or already-occupied garden, wanting the largest enclosed room available from a compact footprint, comfortable arranging base and assembly, using the building seasonally, and budgeting around EUR 7,500 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long boundary run of nearly 9 m, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting to consolidate room, storage and outdoor decking into one structure rather than three, and budgeting around EUR 14,300 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden who currently has, or would otherwise need, a separate shed, wanting to combine storage and a 12.5 m2 room in one structure, comfortable arranging base and assembly, budgeting around EUR 9,170 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long boundary run of nearly 9 m, prepared to seek planning permission, wanting room, storage and sheltered outdoor seating consolidated into one structure, and budgeting around EUR 16,020 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a medium garden and limited existing outbuildings, wanting a 14 m2 room in the supplier's thickest wall specification with a sheltered porch, comfortable arranging base and assembly, budgeting around EUR 11,030 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden and few existing outbuildings, wanting a 19 m2 room in the thickest available wall with a covered veranda facing down the plot, comfortable arranging base and assembly for a heavier 70 mm kit, and budgeting around EUR 11,890 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

SOMEONE WHO WILL WORK IN IT FIVE DAYS A WEEK, ALL YEAR, AND WANTS AN IRISH SUPPLIER THEY CAN VISIT. That combination is unusual and this record meets it: a genuinely insulated envelope, a showroom in three provinces, and a builder who fits the insulation and the interior themselves rather than leaving it to the buyer's trades. THEY ARE REPLACING A SPARE BEDROOM, not adding a summer house. NOT FOR: a buyer comparing this model's square metres against the log models' without asking about the measurement basis; nor for one who needs a U-value to compare against a SIPS or frame-built competitor.

A homeowner with substantial land solving a real housing need — an adult child, ageing parents, or a long-term rental — with roughly EUR 35k-50k available once services and planning are counted. Running this as a proper construction project with a contractor, and choosing All In One Cabins to keep the shell cost down on what is effectively a small house.

A budget-conscious homeowner wanting a summerhouse, hobby room or seasonal workspace for around EUR 10k-15k all-in, with a long narrow strip of garden and no appetite for a big build. Comfortable with a flatpack and hiring a local electrician if the room ever needs power. Not the right pick for daily year-round working — 44mm walls will show in winter heating.

A homeowner adding compact guest accommodation or a small independent unit for roughly EUR 18k-28k all-in, who has a builder and plumber lined up. Suits occasional guests, a visiting family member or a teenager wanting independence. Too tight for permanent full-time living for more than one person.

A HYBRID WORKER WITH A SMALL GARDEN AND A CLEAR SINGLE PURPOSE. They want somewhere warm enough to use in January, they are not trying to fit a gym in, and they would rather keep most of the lawn. A recognised retail brand and a published size make the decision feel low-risk, which is much of the appeal. THEY SHOULD STILL ASK ONE QUESTION: how thick are the walls, and what is the internal dimension — because on a 3 m square that answer changes the furniture layout. NOT FOR: two occupants, or anyone needing storage as well as a desk.

A HOUSEHOLD THAT HAS OUTGROWN THE SPARE ROOM AND WANTS ONE BUILDING TO SOLVE SEVERAL PROBLEMS. Two people working from home on alternating days, or a workspace that has to double as a gym or a teenager's room — the uses that need 4 m of depth rather than 3 m. They have a garden large enough to give up 24 m2 and still keep the required 25 m2 of private open space. THEY MUST CHECK THE COMBINED ALLOWANCE FIRST. NOT FOR: a small garden, or anyone intending to sleep in it — exempted structures permit no human habitation.

A family with children or teenagers who want a supervised-but-separate room in the garden with its own WC, budgeting roughly EUR 11k-20k once plumbing and bathroom fit-out are added. Prioritises self-containment over square metres. Should get the true floor area confirmed in writing before ordering.

A homeowner with a height-restricted or closely overlooked site who needs two bedrooms and a warmer building than the entry-level Ree, budgeting roughly EUR 30k-43k all-in. Choosing this over the Allen or Meelagh only makes sense if the garden genuinely cannot take a larger footprint — otherwise both are better buildings for similar or less money.

A FIRST-TIME BUYER WITH A CLEAR SINGLE PURPOSE AND A CAP ON SPEND. Someone who works from home two or three days a week and needs to get out of the kitchen — not someone building a second living space. They are price-led, they want a number on a page rather than a consultation, and a five-figure entry point is what brings them to this supplier. THEY BENEFIT FROM THE CROSS-BORDER QUOTING: an Irish buyer near the border, or anyone comparing sterling and euro pricing, gets a straight comparison here that most suppliers in this catalogue do not offer. THEY MUST BE HONEST WITH THEMSELVES ABOUT DEPTH: at 2.44 m, this is a one-function room, and buying it expecting two functions is the commonest way to be disappointed by a small garden building.

A homeowner with a long narrow garden strip who needs a self-contained one-bedroom unit and cannot fit anything wider, budgeting roughly EUR 34k-46k all-in. Should ask the supplier directly what justifies the price against the Bofin before committing. Anyone with space for a larger footprint will get considerably more building elsewhere in this range.

Someone working from home three to five days a week who values light and volume over insulation depth, with a square garden position and roughly EUR 12k-18k once electrics are added. Willing to pay for the thicker-wall upgrade if they intend to use it through an Irish winter.

A homeowner building permanent independent accommodation on a large rural or semi-rural site, budgeting roughly EUR 40k-55k once services and planning are counted. Prioritises quality of living space over raw square metres — this is the model to pick if the occupants will actually live there rather than just sleep there.

SOMEONE ADDING A GARDEN SITTING ROOM TO A HOUSEHOLD THAT ALREADY HAS A SHED. The smaller pavilion suits a plot where the allowance is shared, and the leisure brief — light, view, somewhere to sit outside the house without being outdoors — is what distinguishes this buyer from an office one. THEY SHOULD NOT ASSUME A GLAZED PAVILION SITS OUTSIDE THE PLANNING RULES, because a roofed structure counts toward the 30 m2 however it is described. NOT FOR: a working office, where no thermal figures are published; nor for a buyer who wants a confirmed area before enquiring.

A HOUSEHOLD BUYING GARDEN LEISURE RATHER THAN WORKSPACE. Somewhere bright to sit in April and October, entertain in, or watch the garden from — the sun-room requirement, which is genuinely different from an office brief and is why the product exists. THEY ARE MORE LIKELY THAN AN OFFICE BUYER TO SKIP THE PLANNING QUESTION ENTIRELY, treating a glazed pavilion as garden furniture rather than a structure — which is precisely the mistake to avoid, since a roofed structure counts toward the 30 m2 whatever it is called. NOT FOR: year-round working use on current evidence, since no thermal specification is published.

A homeowner creating family or guest accommodation on a genuinely constrained budget — realistically EUR 25k-40k once walls are upgraded, services connected and planning obtained. Willing to trade insulation depth for space and to manage a multi-trade project. Suits seasonal or guest use out of the box; needs the upgrade for permanent occupation.

A homeowner with significant land providing a full family home — relatives, multigenerational living or a three-bed rental — with roughly EUR 45k-60k available once services and planning are counted. Running it as a full construction project with a contractor, architect and planner, and using the flatpack route to control shell cost on what is unambiguously a house.

Unknown on the evidence Atlas holds. Every homeowner profile this cabin would suit is served better and more cheaply by another model in the same range. If the supplier can evidence a specification difference that justifies roughly EUR 1,895 per square metre, that profile may exist — but Atlas will not describe one until the evidence is there.

A FAMILY HOUSING A RELATIVE WHO NEEDS THEIR OWN FRONT DOOR. An elderly parent, or an adult child who cannot find a rental — a genuine housing problem rather than a workspace one, and the reason annexes exist as a category. THEY ARE ENTERING A CONSENT PROCESS, not making a retail purchase, and should budget time and professional advice accordingly. NOT FOR: anyone shopping in the garden-room category expecting exempt development — which is exactly the confusion this product's placement invites, and the reason the record states the position plainly.

An ENGLISH homeowner housing a family member — an adult child, an elderly parent — or creating a long-stay guest annexe, who wants residential-grade accommodation with a kitchen and bathroom and a plastered interior, built to a width that suits their garden rather than to a catalogue size. They value that the building needs no concrete base and can in principle be moved later, and they are the kind of buyer who reads a specification: named insulation products with thicknesses, a named steel supplier, a 25-year structural guarantee. Crucially, they will let BOOTHS fit the kitchen and bathroom rather than their own tradesperson, because doing otherwise cuts the guarantee to one year and fixes the building in place permanently. They accept that heating is a separate purchase and that a site visit and groundworks quotation follow from the plumbing. NOT THIS BUYER: an Irish purchaser — no Irish delivery is published, and the Caravan Act route the supplier relies on does not exist here; anyone who needs a U-value; anyone wanting an incidental garden room rather than accommodation.

SOMEONE WHO WILL WORK IN IT ALL YEAR AND HAS THOUGHT ABOUT JANUARY. They have concluded that a basic cabin will be cold and are prepared to pay more for the envelope rather than for extra square metres — which is the right trade for a room used daily. They are buying from a recognised retail brand and expect a delivered, straightforward product rather than a design process. THEY SHOULD PRESS ON TWO NUMBERS the supplier does not publish: internal dimensions and U-value. NOT FOR: a buyer who needs a large multi-use room, or one comparing purely on price per nominal square metre.

A practical homeowner around the GBP 14k mark who wants real space rather than a premium badge, and who is genuinely willing to get out with timber treatment once a year. Suits a home office, hobby room or garden lounge. A poor fit for anyone who wants to install it and never think about it again — the guarantee depends on the upkeep.

A HOUSEHOLD MAKING WELLNESS THE POINT OF THE GARDEN. They want the full sequence — heat, then water — and they would rather buy it once than assemble it piece by piece over three summers. They have space and budget, and they are likely to be building this instead of, not alongside, a garden office. THAT TRADE IS THE HONEST FRAMING: a combined unit is likely to consume a substantial share of the 30 m2 allowance, so a future workspace may need permission. NOT FOR: a garden already carrying a shed or garage near the limit.

A COMMITTED SAUNA USER WITH A SPECIFIC SPOT IN MIND. They know how many people they want to seat and they have a length of garden — along a fence, beside a patio — that suits a barrel form. Because the product is made to order they are in a specification conversation rather than a purchase, and they should arrive at it already knowing how much of their 30 m2 allowance is unspent. NOT FOR: a buyer who wants a fixed price and a catalogue size, or anyone needing enclosed workspace rather than heat.

A FAMILY OR SOCIABLE HOUSEHOLD BUILDING AN OUTDOOR WELLNESS CORNER. They want capacity for guests, they like the ritual of a wood fire, and they are content to manage fuel and water rather than press a button. They are not comparing this with a garden office and should not be shown one as an equivalent. THEY SHOULD THINK ABOUT THE DECKING NOW, because that is where the planning question actually arises. NOT FOR: anyone needing enclosed, weatherproof floor space.

A BUYER BROWSING A LARGE RANGE AND DRAWN TO A NAME THEY LIKE. That is an honest description of how this product would be chosen, because nothing published distinguishes it on function, size or specification. THEY WILL NEED A CONVERSATION RATHER THAN A CATALOGUE, and the first question is what the Plus designation actually covers. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, since Estonia-only shipping leaves no purchasing route; nor for anyone building a shortlist from published specifications, where this record contributes nothing testable.

SOMEONE WHO HAS SEEN THE TONIO IN PERSON AND WANTS THE BIGGER ONE. With nothing published to compare, that is realistically the only way this decision gets made — which places the whole weight of the purchase on the supplier conversation and, ideally, a showroom visit. THEY SHOULD ASK FOR BOTH MODELS' FOOTPRINTS SIDE BY SIDE, since the numbering alone establishes nothing. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for anyone whose garden is close to its allowance, where an unmeasured larger model is the least defensible choice.

A BELFAST-AREA BUYER WHO WILL VISIT AND DECIDE ON THE DAY. Someone who is choosing between two models by standing in both of them rather than by reading specifications, and who is content to take the size and build details from the salesperson rather than from a website. THEY SHOULD STILL LEAVE WITH NUMBERS: an external footprint, a ridge height and a written note of what the price includes, because none of it exists in published form. NOT FOR: a Republic of Ireland buyer working remotely, who faces both a different planning regime and a record that cannot be tested; or anyone whose shortlist method is a spreadsheet.

SOMEONE WHO WANTS TO SEE IT BEFORE THEY BUY IT. A buyer within reach of Belfast who distrusts brochures, prefers to walk into a finished building and ask questions face to face, and is comfortable getting the specification verbally rather than from a website. That is a legitimate and often sensible way to buy a garden room, and this supplier is set up for it. NOT FOR: a homeowner in the Republic who wants to compare products remotely, because nothing here can be compared on paper and the planning regime differs; or anyone who needs published dimensions to plan a base, a budget or an exemption check before travelling.

SOMEONE BUILDING A SECOND DWELLING ON THEIR SITE AND TREATING IT AS SUCH. A family housing two relatives, a rural landowner adding accommodation, or a self-builder using a log kit as the shell — all legitimate, all requiring a full application. THEY HAVE OR WILL ENGAGE A DESIGNER, and the building is one component of a project rather than a purchase. NOT FOR: anyone shopping in the garden-room category expecting exempt development — which is precisely the confusion this product's placement invites, and the reason the record spells the position out.

A homeowner with a large open garden, prepared to seek planning permission, who needs two distinct enclosed spaces and is willing to ask the supplier for the internal dimensions and for what occupies the remainder of the envelope before ordering, budgeting around EUR 14,300 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

A homeowner with a clear garden and no existing outbuildings, who needs two distinct spaces rather than one open room, is prepared to ask the supplier for the internal dimensions before ordering, and is budgeting around EUR 14,730 for the delivered kit before groundworks.

NONE. This record identifies neither a building nor a supplier, so there is no homeowner it can be matched to, and constructing a profile from the word 'Ultimate' would be pure invention. THE ONLY USEFUL STATEMENT is a negative one, and it is worth making plainly: a homeowner encountering this entry in a listing is looking at a catalogue artefact rather than a purchasable product, and should disregard it. Its value to Atlas is as a flagged defect awaiting reconciliation, not as decision intelligence.

Someone who works from the room every day, year-round, and cares more about being warm in February and cheap to heat than about square metres. Comfortable at roughly GBP 19k for a small building. Typically a remote professional, or a homeowner who has researched insulation properly and wants evidence rather than adjectives.

A UK homeowner who has costed the whole life of the building rather than just the purchase, and who would rather pay more once than re-stain timber every few years. Often someone with a small, overlooked garden where the studio is permanently in view from the house. Comfortable at roughly GBP 16,000 for a compact room, and more interested in finish quality and thermal specification than in maximising square metres.

A FAMILY LOOKING FOR EXTRA ROOM AND NOT YET SURE WHETHER ANYONE WILL SLEEP IN IT. That ambiguity is the defining feature of this buyer, and it is the thing they most need resolved — a day room for teenagers or guests is incidental use and permitted; a bedroom is not, at any size. THEY ARE PRICE-CONSCIOUS AND BUYING FROM A RETAILER, so they will not have a designer to raise the question for them. NOT FOR: anyone planning overnight accommodation while relying on the garden-structure exemption — that is the specific mistake this record exists to prevent.

CANNOT BE CHARACTERISED FROM HELD EVIDENCE. Without a size, a price, a specification or a route to purchase in Ireland, there is no honest way to describe the buyer this product suits, and no profile has been constructed from the design imagery alone. THE ONLY THING THAT CAN BE SAID: a homeowner who pursues this product will be running a cross-border direct enquiry with a Belgian studio, arranging their own delivery, base and installation, and taking responsibility for Irish planning compliance themselves. That is a project-management undertaking rather than a purchase, and it suits someone with the time and appetite for it.

A HOUSEHOLD WITH A NARROW GARDEN AND ONE THING TO PUT IN IT. Where a 4 × 4 m or 5 × 4 m building would dominate or simply not fit, a 5 × 3 m along the boundary gives a full-length room and leaves the lawn intact — and half the allowance besides. THEY WILL USE IT FOR ONE PURPOSE, most often a desk. NOT FOR: a household wanting two uses in one building, where the depth defeats them; nor for a buyer who needs the construction settled before making contact.

SOMEONE WHOSE GARAGE HAS FILLED UP. Bicycles, tools, half-finished projects and the mower — a practical building for a practical problem, and the most ordinary requirement a garden structure serves. THEY WANT DURABILITY AND SPACE RATHER THAN GLAZING, and they are unlikely to be troubled by the use condition, since none of the work is paid. NOT FOR: a home business, where the incidental-use condition becomes live; nor for an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published; nor for a workspace needing year-round comfort, where nothing thermal is specified.

A COMMITTED HOME MAKER WITH REAL EQUIPMENT. A bench, a saw, a dust extractor and somewhere to stack materials — the point at which a shed stops being adequate and a workshop becomes the right category. THEY ARE ALSO THE BUYER MOST LIKELY TO DRIFT TOWARD PAID WORK, which is worth flagging while the building is still a plan rather than a fact. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds; nor for a garden already carrying structures, where an unmeasured mid-sized building is a poor bet against the combined allowance.

A MAKER WITH MACHINERY — someone whose practice needs floor space for equipment, racking for materials and room to work around a project rather than over a bench. That is a genuine and under-served requirement, and the top of a workshop line is where it belongs. THEY ARE THE BUYER FOR WHOM THE USE QUESTION IS LEAST ACADEMIC, because a workshop at this scale is often where a hobby turns into a business. NOT FOR: an Irish homeowner, on availability; nor for a garden with existing structures, where the allowance arithmetic cannot be checked.

A SERIOUS AMATEUR WOODWORKER — someone with a bench, hand tools and a machine or two, working for their own satisfaction rather than for customers. That distinction is not pedantic: it is the line the exemption draws, and this buyer sits on the right side of it. THEY NEED DURABILITY AND POWER MORE THAN THEY NEED WINDOWS, which is what a workshop-named product should deliver. NOT FOR: anyone making for sale, where the use condition becomes live; nor for an Irish homeowner, since no purchasing route is published.

A HOBBYIST METALWORKER OR MAKER WITH A GENUINE CRAFT PRACTICE. Someone whose work needs a hard-wearing space, ventilation and tolerance of noise — and who is doing it for themselves rather than for customers, which is what keeps the exemption available. THEY WILL HAVE SPECIFIC TECHNICAL QUESTIONS the catalogue cannot answer, and should expect to raise them with the supplier and, on fire and insurance, with their insurer. NOT FOR: commercial work, which changes the planning route; nor for an Irish homeowner, on availability grounds.

NO TYPICAL HOMEOWNER CAN BE DESCRIBED FROM THE EVIDENCE HELD, and describing one would be an invention this standard exists to prevent. There is no confirmed size, no confirmed specification, no confirmed price and no verified delivery coverage to match a buyer against. WHAT CAN BE SAID: the only person for whom this record is currently useful is someone who has ALREADY SEEN the product elsewhere — at a show, in person, through a recommendation — and wants to know what Atlas holds. The answer is a turnkey service span, an undefined lifetime warranty, and an unread website. Their next step is a direct enquiry seeking a stated floor area in square metres, a written construction specification, a U-value if one exists, the warranty document with its definition of 'lifetime', a clear answer on whether foundations sit inside the turnkey price, and confirmation of delivery to their county. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone comparing products on published evidence, which is the normal way of buying a garden room and is not possible here.

Someone choosing a garden building as much for its FORM as its function — a hexagonal pavilion-like room to be seen from the house, with sightlines in several directions, rather than a rectangular box at the end of the lawn. They are prepared to run the enquiry themselves: telephone or email the supplier, obtain a stated floor area in square metres, a construction specification, a U-value if one exists, the warranty document and a clear answer on whether the base is inside the turnkey price. They are comfortable that Atlas can confirm none of that, because the supplier's site cannot be read. NOT THIS BUYER, and this is most people: anyone who wants to compare specifications before making contact, since no comparison is possible; anyone who needs to test the 30 m2 planning allowance, which cannot be tested without an area; anyone for whom running cost matters, given that the hexagonal form carries proportionally more wall per square metre and the insulation is unspecified.

Someone with a small garden who needs one desk and has already encountered this supplier directly — at a show, through a recommendation, or by a site visit — rather than by comparing published specifications, which is not possible here. They are prepared to run the enquiry themselves and know exactly what to ask for: the external footprint in square metres, the wall, roof and floor build-up, a U-value if one exists, the warranty document with its definition of 'lifetime', whether the base sits inside the turnkey price, and confirmation of delivery to their county. They understand that on a very small building the envelope is proportionally more important, not less, so the missing specification is the first thing they will chase. NOT THIS BUYER: anyone comparing compact offices on published evidence — several suppliers in this Atlas publish areas, prices and specifications for buildings of this scale and this one publishes none; anyone who needs the planning position settled before making contact.

A FAMILY TREATING THE GARDEN ROOM AS AN EXTENSION OF THE HOUSE. Two workspaces, or a workspace plus a gym or playroom — 24 m2 usable with 4 m of depth is enough to zone the room properly. They are spending seriously and expect the building to serve several purposes over several years. THEY MUST BE THE KIND OF BUYER WHO CHECKS TWO NUMBERS RATHER THAN ONE: the footprint against their remaining allowance, and the finished height against 3 m. Yardbox gives them both figures, which is why this product suits a careful buyer and penalises a casual one. NOT FOR: a garden that already holds a shed or garage, where the combined total would breach the limit; or a buyer unwilling to consider a planning application if the site turns out to be tighter than expected.

A HOUSEHOLD MAKING THE GARDEN ROOM THEIR PRIMARY WORKSPACE. Someone working from home most of the week who needs room for a proper desk, storage and a second chair — or a couple sharing the room at different times of day. They have concluded that a 9 m2 pod would be outgrown within a year, and they are prepared to spend more to avoid that. THEY ARE EVIDENCE-LED BUYERS: they will notice that this supplier publishes footprint, usable area and height, and they will use those figures to check the planning position and set out the base themselves. NOT FOR: a garden already carrying a large garage or shed, where 16.64 m2 leaves little margin; or a buyer whose deciding factor is documented thermal performance, which is not held.

A METHODICAL FIRST-TIME BUYER WHO READS THE NUMBERS. Someone working from home two or three days a week who wants a proper room rather than a shed conversion, who intends to check the planning position themselves, and who will be reassured by a supplier that publishes footprint, usable area and height rather than one that publishes a photograph. THEY ARE OFTEN COMPARING THREE OR FOUR OPTIONS ON A SPREADSHEET — and this is one of the few records in the catalogue that can fill every column. THEY VALUE PROXIMITY: a Co. Down supplier serving both jurisdictions means delivery, installation and aftercare are realistic rather than theoretical. NOT FOR: a household needing two functions in one room, or a buyer who needs published U-values and a warranty term before committing.

SOMEONE BUYING AN OBJECT AS MUCH AS A ROOM. Design-led, willing to import, and drawn to the mirrored envelope rather than to a specification sheet — in practice more often a hospitality or short-let operator than a homeowner needing a garden office. THEY WILL BE COMFORTABLE RUNNING THEIR OWN PLANNING AND SITING PROCESS, because the supplier publishes nothing that would do it for them. NOT FOR: a homeowner who needs a defensible floor area and height for an exemption check; nor for anyone wanting a documented, delivered, Irish-supported product.

NOT A HOMEOWNER AT ALL, ON THE EVIDENCE — A GLAMPING OR SHORT-STAY OPERATOR. Someone with a site, a hospitality business and a planning process already in hand, for whom a distinctive mirrored unit is a commercial asset. THAT IS THE HONEST ANSWER, and it is more useful than pretending the product suits a suburban garden. THE HOMEOWNER WHO SHOULD READ THIS RECORD is the one who found the product while shopping for a garden room and needs to know why it is a different category of purchase. NOT FOR: incidental domestic use, which is the only use the exemption permits.

SOMEONE WITH A PRIVATE, WELL-SCREENED OR RURAL SITE AND A VIEW WORTH FRAMING. The product only makes sense where the glazing is an asset rather than a liability, which rules out most overlooked suburban gardens — and the buyer who understands that is the buyer this suits. They are design-led, comfortable importing, and treating the building as an experience rather than as workspace. NOT FOR: a terraced or semi-detached garden with close neighbours; nor for anyone needing predictable year-round thermal comfort on published figures.

SOMEONE WHOSE SITE IS TEMPORARY OR UNCERTAIN — a rented property, land awaiting development, or a business testing a location. Relocatability is worth paying for only if it will actually be used; for a permanent back garden it adds cost and regulatory ambiguity without benefit. THIS BUYER IS ALSO USUALLY TAKING PROFESSIONAL PLANNING ADVICE ALREADY, which is what the unresolved regime question requires. NOT FOR: a homeowner installing a permanent garden office, who would be better served by a fixed structure with a published footprint and a clear exemption route.

A DESIGN-LED BUYER WITH A MODEST GARDEN who wants the mirrored look without the footprint of the larger forms. They are more likely than the Big Monolith buyer to be an actual homeowner rather than an operator, which is precisely why the height limit matters to them: a suburban garden makes the 3 m test live in a way a rural site does not. THEY SHOULD EXPECT TO DO THEIR OWN VERIFICATION, since the supplier publishes nothing that would settle it. NOT FOR: a homeowner who needs certainty before ordering, or who cannot import from Estonia.

A BUYER WHO CAME TO ÖÖD FOR THE DESIGN AND WILL START WITH THE BEST-KNOWN MODEL. They have usually seen the mirrored units in a hospitality or holiday setting and want the same object at home; they are willing to import from Estonia and to manage siting themselves.
